LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 73) to provide for the government inspection of vessels. He said:	This Bill is to apply
to vessels not now inspected under the Dominion Inspection Act. At present, all well found vessels are inspected, but barges, which have no motive power, are not inspected. Clauses 6 and 7 of this Bill provide that the present Inspection and Equipment Act shall apply to small steam vessels over five tons. The matter has been discussed by the divisional court of Ontario, as will be found in 120 Ontario Reports, page 154, Sturgeon vs. Port Bur-well Fishing Company. The representatives of a man who was drowned were not able to recover from the steamer notwithstanding the fact that there was no boat or axe on board. The life buoy was fastened too securely for quick use. Had this vessel been equipped as others must be under the law, the life of the man would have been saved. Clause 8 of the Bill is to provide that vessels towing shall carry a rocket gun. At present, steel boats cannot get within reach of their tows which have broken loose, where the sea is very high. The American Steel Trust require all their vessels to carry rocket guns, not because it is provided by law, but for the protection of the Trust's own interests. Ocean vessels are required by law to carry these appliances. The cost is very small.
Would this apply everywhere?
Yes, all over the Dominion.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before that motion is carried and in view of the orders in council that were brought down yesterday in connection with the issue of capital stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I must again trespass for a short time on the forbearance of the House. It is now apparent from those orders in council that the capital issued under the original charter of the Canadian Pacific Railway was $65,000,000; that in 1902 under the Act of parliament embodying an order in council, its capitalization was increased by $20,000,000; and in an Act of parliament, and in the order in council, provision was made, first, that the issue should not be for less than par; second, that
the money was not to be used for any purpose other than contained in the resolution of the shareholders; and third, that this issue was to be excluded from the operation of what is called the ten per cent clause in the original charter. In 1904 another order in council was passed, increasing the capital stock by $25,000,000; that order in council was put through council by the present Minister of Finance, but for some reason or other the order in council is somewhat different. It provides certainly that the stock shall not be issued for less than par, it also provides that the proceeds of that stock shall not be issued for works outside of Canada; but it does not provide that that stock shall be removed from the application of the ten per cent clause. So far as I know, no Act of parliament was passed confirming the issue. In 1906 the stock was increased by $40,000,000. A provision for its issue at not less than par is in the order in council, and that the money shall not be used outside of Canada is in the order in council, it is also in the order in council that the stock so authorized shall not come under the ten per cent clause. Now in 1908 another order in council has been issued for an increase of capital stock by $50,000,000, making the total issue by this company of capital stock of $200,000,000. In other words, within the last six years the capital stock has been increased by $135,000,000. I cannot say whether in that time any bonds have been issued. But the significant thing is that within the last six years after the road had practically been constructed, after its transcontinental character had been assured, and when that had been done on $65,000 000 of stock, they have in the last six years increased that capital stock by $135,000,000, an annual increase of about $15,000,000 a year. If this stock is issued at par, as it has been, and it would bring on the average, as it would have brought, 165, or 65 premium, we have allowed the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway to distribute a bonus equal to $9,000,000 a year for the past six years, besides the dividends they have paid. If this is sound financing, this method will be continued, and year after year, we will have this great company issuing this stock, and ' cutting these melons,' as it is called, and distributing besides their dividends, over $9,000,000 a year among the shareholders.
Now let me explain to the House and to the country how these things work out, what follows on an order in council of this kind. The shareholders' capital was, until this last order in council passed, $150,000,r 000, and they were allowed to issue $50,000,000 of new stock. Now what takes place is this: As soon as they have this authority, this permission the Canadian Pacific Railway treasurer, or other official, sends a letter to every shareholder and says that in

view of the recent authorization the capital stock has been increased bv $50,000,000, and that the shareholder is entitled, has a right to one new share for every three old shares. So if a shareholder happens to own three hundred shares of old stock he has a right to take up an additional one hundred shares at par, and this document which he receives from the railway company is technically called a right. And what must the shareholder do who has this right ?
Does he go to the treasurer's office and say: I am entitled to this 100 additional shares and here is my cheque for $10,000? He hardly ever does that, he runs to his broker and says: Here is my right entitling me to 100 shares of Canadian Pacific; sell it for me to-morrow. The broker sells the piece of paper, entitling the shareholder to 100 shares for from $6,500 to $7,500; the shareholder puts that money in his pocket, he does not pay even the par value of the stock, but the man who buys the right, after paying the $6,500 for the benefit of the shareholder, has to go to the treasurer's office and pay the $10,000 par value of the shares. Thus these documents, these rights, secure what is called the cutting of the melon and that apparently is the new kind of railroad financing we are to have in Canada in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, that every year or at the most two years, there is to be this melon to be cut, this increase of capital stock, this dealing in rights; and apparently it has been so profitable to the shareholder of the Canadian Pacific Railway that now they have ceased issuing bonds when they require capital for the purposes of their railroad and issue stock in this way, sell the rights and reap enormous profit from the transaction. To whom is this distribution, this $35,000,000 free gift made? Does it go to Canadians? No, most of it goes to men outside of our country, and Canada presents a spectacle of every year making a free bonus gift of $9,000,000 to shareholders in one of our propositions, most of whom live out of our country. We this year have only $100,000 to give to the sufferers in Italy, but every year we have $9,000,000 of free cash bonus to give to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If this is good policy and can be justified, it will probably be continued. If there is nothing wrong about it we ought to continue it. No wonder the reputation of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the monetary centres of the world is very high. Any one's financial reputation can easily be maintained in that way if this kind of financing is allowed.
I wish now to go back to the original basis of the authorization of capital stock to railroads and see whether this practice, which has recently been introduced into Canada, is one that can be justified. My view of the position is that whenever and Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
wherever parliament charters and grants a franchise to a railway company, it grants to that company certain powers for the purposes of the undertaking, either expressly or by implication. Among the powers so given is the right to issue securities such as stocks, bonds, debentures, &c. This power of issue is a trust that must be honestly and faithfully administered for the purposes of the undertaking and for all parties interested, including the public who are to be served by the railroad. In other words if we have created a railway company and given it power to issue certificates there is implied in the charter an understanding that these certificates shall be issued only for the purposes of the undertaking; these certificates are not to be used as a bonus for the people who happen to own the shares of the railroad. I say that is the underlying principle which should govern the incorporation of these companies, and I think parliament will still hold that view when it is brought clearly before them. Parliament undertook to regulate the amount and mode of issue of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the original charter granted in 1881. In 1892, while the Conservatives were in power, the company was empowered to issue further shares of capital stock for any purpose for which the company required new capital, such issue being first approved by order in council, and the fourth section of the Act of 1892 provides:
The proceeds of each issue of shares of capital stock shall he applied by the company exclusively to the purposes for which the shareholders authorized such issue.
In other words it is expressly provided in one of these Acts that the whole proceeds-and by proceeds I mean all that the security will bring-must he applied expressly to the object for which it was voted, for the furtherance of the undertaking, whatever it may happen to be. My contention is that the Governor in Council, as trustees for the people and for parliament, were bound before they approved of any issue of stock, to see that it would be issued to the best advantage of all parties concerned, the public included. That is to say, if the stock to be authorized would bring more than par, it should be so stipulated in the order in council. It was well known that these securities would bring more than par and that the underlying principle of parliament regulating and authorizing the issue of securities is that the proceeds of them must go to the undertaking. If that is so a mistake has been made, a wrong has been committed; this wrong ought to be righted and certainly it ought never to be allowed to occur again in this country.

Does my hon. friend say that there is any evidence that

the proceeds from the sales of these shares were not applied in the interest of the undertaking or the development of the enterprise?

Technically the hon. gentleman gets around my point, as the proceeds of the share may be really the $100 the man pays for it after the right has been melted and the $65 has been put in his pocket, and my hon. friend may have a nice point in arguing that the proceeds of the issue are only what goes into the treasury. I say the proceeds of the issue are everything that could be got out of it, and it ought all to be consecrated to the undertaking.

Does my hon. friend mean to say that he has any evidence that the proceeds of these shares were not applied for the regular purposes and in good faith in the interest of the organization?
cil, but so far I have not been able to get a copy of it.
Is the last order in council not down?

Not the one passed in 1902. The orders in council increasing the capital have been brought down, but the order in council mentioned by the late Minister of the Interior providing for an immediate reference to some tribunal to ascertain the capital actually expended in the road has .not yet come down.

I did not understand my hon. friend to ask for that order in council. He asked me about it and I told him I would make inquiry of the Minister of Justice concerning the situation of the case referred to the Supreme Court. If such order in council exists it can be brought down quite easily.

Yes, I undertake to say that for every share of Canadian Pacific Railway that has been sold in, recent years, while $100 went into the treasury, anything from $60 to $70 went into the pockets of the then owners of shares.
Turning to the question of tolls and capital actually expended in the road, the original charter of the Canadian Pacific Railway provided for the regulation of the tolls on that road. It also provided for the regulation of the profit and net revenue of the road. Clearly parliament provided for the regulation of tolls and this was based on what is called the 10 per cent clause. In other words, in the original charter, while parliament theretofore had reserved to itself the right to say that no railway shall earn more than 15 per cent on the capital invested, they said; in view of many concessions to the Canadian Pacific Railway we shall make a, provision that its profits shall not exceed 10 per cent on its capital stock, and the moment it does exceed that somebody can step in, (then the Railway Committee of the Privy Council) and reduce the rates charged by the railway. And so parliament in the original Act expressly provided for the regulation of the rates and stipulated that in no case should the rates be such that the net profits of that road exceed 10 per cent on the money actually expended on the construction of the road.
The first great question to he determined in dealing with a railroad of this kind is whether the time has yet arrived for reducing the tolls which may be charged, and as far as I can gather nothing has yet been done although, according to the statement of the late Minister of the Interior, made in this House in 1902, an order in council was at that time passed for that purpose. I have asked the Minister of Railways to bring down that order in coun-

Then we may get it later on if the minister cares to give it. if the railway could show that it was not earning a fair return on the capital expended it could complain of any attempt to reduce its rates, and I am not arguing just now that the rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway ought to be reduced, but I do propose to assert that in view of that original provision we should know how much money has actually been expended by this road, notwithstanding the fact that the operation of that clause has been removed from a number of these recent orders in council. I go on the assumption, therefore, in order to secure the lowest possible tolls to the public who use the road, it is of prime importance that parliament or the Governor in Council who authorized or approved of the issue of capital (whether stock, bonds or other securities), should see that any and all ' capital actually expended in the construction of the road ' is raised in the least expensive manner, is raised in the most provident manner; that not an unnecessary dollar of debt is incurred or of high interestbearing obligation is issued as against a low interest-bearing obligation wherever possible, and that the highest possible value is obtained for any such security, and that the entire and highest possible proceeds of any such issue goes into the treasury of the road for the purposes for which it was authorized-that on no pretext whatever shall the best possible proceeds of these issues be diverted. To divert any of them is, I hold, criminal; it is to be guilty of malversation of funds, is a breach of trust and a violation of the sacred obligation on the part of the company to give the best possible and cheapest service in consideration of the many valuable things given it by the state, in the way of lands, money, exemption privileges, &c. If, therefore, $30,000,000 of stock issued at $165 would produce what it

will produce in the open market, namely, $50,000,000, and if the proceeds go into the treasury, the government was bound to authorize only that amount and to stipulate that it be sold at the highest amount it would bring. In other words the $50,000,000 could be got for $30,000,000 stock, the tolls charged on which could not exceed 10 per cent or $3,000,000 a year. Instead of this it will be on this last issue 10 per cent on $50,000,000 or $5,000,000 a year, or an unnecessary tax of $2,000,000 on the people of Canada. In other words $30,000,000 of stock issued at the market price would have produced $50,000,000, and as the dividend which would be allowed to the company would be 10 per cent on that $30,000,000, it would amount to only $3,000,000 a year, instead of which you have allowed them to issue $50,000,000 which is entitled to earn 10 per cent and which means $5,000,000 a year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not at all.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him this question?
Yes.

In the face of the order in council which says absolutely that the 10 per cent shall not be calculated on this amount at all, how does the hon. gentleman argue that it is to be calculated on that amount?

I am coming to that. The tolls of the company are limited to 10 per cent on its capital, and as a matter of fact to-day the tolls of the company are 10 per cent;-the net earnings of the company to-day are 10 per cent on the capital stock and the company is going to see that it always will be 10 per cent on the capital stock as long as it has the right to do so.
On the original capital stock?

Yes. Now I come to the minister in this: That the company is entitled to a fair return on its stock issue or on any money put into securities of tbe road, and if $50,000,000 is to be earned upon, when $30,000,000 would do, I say an injustice is done to the people who use the road. That is a point I make against the minister; not so much that he has that provision in the statute as that I shall show that the charges upon the traffic of the road would have been much less if that stock had not been sold at par. But, before the government authorized the issue of any further capital I contend it was bound to do two things: first, to scrutinize the reasons advanced and the objects given for the request for additional capital, and second, to examine the treasury of the company and its resources with a view of ascertaining whether it could not provide for the new undertaking out of any resources then in hand, and any unexhausted portions of the immense money and Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
land grants given to the company by the state, or out of the bond-issuing powers of the company as provided or as might be provided by law. Before ever they should have allowed the issue of additional stock, I say it was the duty of the government to examine into the purposes for which the money was to be used, but still more important to examine the treasury of the company and to see whether it had any other resources which could be applied to the object in hand. And the land, and the money grants which were given to the Canadian Pacific Railway were given for the purposes of the undertaking and are so set out in the original documents and were so stated in parliament. They were not given to be used as a hoarding or as a great reserve fund for the road, and they were not given for the purpose of injuring another company. And when the company asked for these powers to issue additional capital they should have shown to the government that they had little or none of these grants in hand. The fact is, on the contrary, they had 13,000,000 acres of land worth at least $150,000,000, and they had bond-issuing powers for a large amount at low interest, or they could get them. I do not know that the government made any such examination. They passed the request of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy on the mere stipulation of a stock issue at par. Now the company at that time, as I have said, had these 13,000,000 acres of land; they had a full treasury, and before they were allowed to issue the stock the government should have said to them: Have you exhausted the resources that parliament has given you already; if you have what have you done with all that money; what have you done, especially with that land? But the Canadian Pacific ' Railway Company were not asked for that; they were allowed to issue this new stock and to-day they are cutting this melon and they are dividing these profits amongst themselves, when at this very moment they have 13,000,000 acres of land out of their original land grant which have not been used. What are they keeping this land for? First of all they are keeping it as a reserve fund, which is improper, and they are using it-

Before my hon. friend leaves that point-does he seriously intend to argue that the order in council should provide for the disposition of stock dependent upon the fluctuating value of the stock market which might be below par one day and above par the next?

Yes, I will come to that and I will give several specific instances. For instance, in the city of Toronto we have the so-called Consumer's Gas Company which undertook to be a partner with the city in the old days and gradually got away from that, but some time ago the city said to the legislature: Inasmuch as

the charges this Gas Company imposes upon the public are to be earned on the basis of 10 per cent on the stock issue, we want you to see that the stock is sold for the highest possible amount that it will bring in the open market. And legislation was passed to that effect, and it has worked out in this way, that whereas a few years ago the company used to sell its stock at $185 it is now selling it and sold it the other day in Toronto at over $200, which is a premium of $100 on every $100 share. That could be attained in Canada in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. 1 venture to say that if you put an advertisement in the financial papers of London to morrow that bids would be received for $50,000,000 ;of Canadian Pacific Railway stock you would get 160 for the whole $50,000,000.
The government were bound for other reasons to investigate the use or lack of use of the land grant. This great Canadian Northwest, which now has ten members from Saskatchewan, seven from Alberta and ten from Manitoba, has been coming to this House year after year and making complaint of two things. It has been complaining first of the exemption of the lands from municipal taxation for twenty years after the Crown grant unless the lands are sold. None of these Canadian Pacific Railway lands in the west have to pay municipal taxes unless they are sold or until the twenty years have expired. As a consequence, the municipalities all over the west complain of this harsh treatment as a great grievance of the people. Another complaint made in the west against the Canadian Pacific Railway is that it is to-day refusing to sell the lands which it owns alongside of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, in order that these two roads, which are intended to serve the country, shall have no local traffic to assist them in carrying out their undertakings. If that is true-and I leave it to the members from the Northwest to say whether it is true or not-that the Canadian Pacific Railway has still an immense amount of property under exemption and is refusing to sell its lands because these rival railroads might be benefited, it is the duty of somebody to see that that condition of affairs is removed. My contention is that not only should the company be compelled to sell these lands in order to raise money for its own needs, but that the government should have used that opportunity to compel it to sell them in order to do away with this exemption clause and prevent this refusal to sell lands because their sale might benefit the two rival roads. That is a question on which the people of the Northwest are the judges. So far as I can gather-I cannot quite gather it in this House-the people of the west believe that, before any power to increase the capital stock of the
Canadian Pacific Railway should have been given, the company should have been compelled to exhaust whatever resources it had in its treasury for the construction of new lines, and should also have been compelled to sell these lands because that would remove the exemption clause and promote settlement along the new lines of railway.
I am not going into the political issue further than to say that I have read within the last two or three days a summary of the history of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as narrated in a book written by Mr. Willison; and it is set out there that one of the greatest grievances of the people in the west was this exemption clause and the hardship it brought upon the poor settler, in the fact that he was for ever tied up not only to a monopoly but to an unjustifiable system of exemption.
I contend still further that the government was bound to have ascertained, if money must be got for securities to be issued, what kind of securities would bear least on the traffic-bonds or debentures. Bonds can be issued at 4 per cent; and my contention is that if the company had to get money after it had exhausted its resources, then it was bound to obtain that money on securities which would have the least possible incidence on the income of the company. In other words, if freight rates must be regulated by the fixed charges, then it is the duty of parliament to see that the fixed charges are of the lowest kind and the charges that are of the lowest kind in connection with railway construction, especially in the case of a successful railway like the Canadian Pacific Railway, are bonds or debenture stock, and not common stock. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company can get all the money it needs at 4 per cent. Instead of that, it is issuing stock that can bear 10 per cent, and at the same time it is distributing $9,000,000 a year as a bonus among its shareholders.
But, some gentlemen say, bonds must bear their interest, and this must be paid, whether the road succeeds or not. There is something in that in the case of a new road; but in the case of an old road like the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is paying its dividends and fixed charges every year, and which can pay 10 per cent on its common stock, surely it can pay 4 per cent on bonds. Fifty million dollars of bonds would have provided the money needed. These would have required $2,000,000 a year for interest, whereas $50,000,000 of stock at 10 per cent requires $5,000,000 a year. The difference is therefore $3,000,000 a year, an unnecessary and perpetual charge on the public, which,1 could be capitalized at $75,000,000. That is rather a serious loss to the people of this country who use the railroads. If this stock issue is justifiable, we

ought to continue it; and it is evidently the policy of the company to quit the issue of bonds, to withhold the sale of its lands, to cut a melon as often as the government or parliament will permit. If the government is right, it ought to have) no hesitation in not only justifying what it has done, but declaring that it will repeat the authorization to-morrow, without condition, examination or departure from the past. What company will issue bonds that can cut a melon on stock every year in addition to a 7 per cent dividend? In other words, there is now 7 per cent interest on the stock and $9,000,000 a year as a bonus distributed among the shareholders. If that is right, it should be continued, and there should never be another issue of bonds on the road, but only common stock. And the surprising thing is that when the company is allowed to issue common stock in this way, how much it wants to issue. For many years it got along with $65,000,000; but $135,000,000 of additional stock has now to be taken care of by the traffic which goes over the road.
Another thing I want to point out. It has been in the newspapers, and a great deal of dust has been tried to be thrown in the eyes of the public, in the attempt to show that there is some connection between this issue of stock and the 10 .per cent clause in the company's charter, and that therefore the exemption must be allowed to continue. There is no connection between the 10 per cent clause and the authorization of the issue of stock. The only stock that was authorized was the $65,000,000 in connection with the 10 per cent clause. That has long ago been exhausted, and the Act of parliament of 1892, under which this stock is issued by order in council, can be repealed to-morrow. It does not apply to the charter at all; and my question to-day is: Is that Act of 1892 to be repealed, and is this process of issuing stock in this way to be continued, or is it to be stopped; and is it to be laid down as the policy underlying the conduct of parliament hereafter, that the issue of all stock shall be a matter of trust and that it will be the duty of parliament or of somebody to see that the character of the security issued shall be such as will carry the lowest interest and therefore be the least burdensome on the traffic? If we can cut down the interest charges on the capital of railways to four or five per cent instead of ten per cent on a lot of it, can we not reduce their passenger and freight rates? If we tell the great Canadian Pacific Railway that they must sell all their land before they are allowed to issue new stock, they will have to sell those lands to the people and in this way we will get rid of these tax exemptions. If they are ordered to sell the lands they own, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern will have settlers all along their lines in localities where there is at present not a settler for Mr. W.
