miles, but the Canadian Pacific Railway refuse to take $20 per acre for land alongside the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern. We must not forget that this Canadian Pacific Railway charter is not altogether a holy thing which cannot be touched. It has been changed a good many times in this House under conditions of one kind or another. The principle was laid down in this House some years ago and with good reasons, that if concessions are to be given the Canadian Pacific Railway, some concessions ought to be exacted from them in return. If they are to be allowed to increase their capital stock, why should they not be ordered to sell their land, and why should they not be compelled to give the people of Canada a two-cent per mile transportation rate, just as they give it to the people of the United States and to the traffic over their lines which originates in the United States? If they give that concession to Americans, why should they not not give it to Canadians as well? But there is to be no two-cent a mile rate for Canadians, who have to sweat in order that millions should go every year to the foreign shareholders, and that will continue just so long as the people of Canada are willing to submit to that kind of thing. Any one who wishes to get further history of the finances of the.Canadian Pacific Railway and how they were handled, had better read th s book to which I have referred ? Mr. Blake was able to point out in this very House, in one of the early discussions on the charter. that of the $65,000,000 of the capital stock issued, only $31,000,000 was realized by the company. And of their $31,000,000 $24,000,000 was paid back to the shareholders in dividends before a dollar had been earned bv the road. In other words, Mr. Blake describes how these original owners of the Canadian Pacific Railway got for many a year twenty-four per cent and then twenty per cent on their investment in that original stock.
That stock had to be sold at less than par. It was sold for fifty per cent less than its face value. Why then, in the name of all that is just and fair, when that stock has gone to a premium, when every $100 of it can be sold at $170, should not that premium go into the Canadian Pacific Railway treasury and be there used for the reduction of its tolls instead^ of being given to the shareholders for their own aggrandizement. If the original stock was sold at this sacrifice, surely it is fair, when the tide has turned and the road proved a great success, that the whole proceeds of any new stock issued should go into the Canadian Pacific Railway treasury for the benefit of the undertaking.
I am not prepared just now to say how much further I shall go into this matter until I see this order in council which has been referred to. In a certain sense, it

does not bear on the issue. We are under no obligation, by the original charter to continue this practice of allowing this great railway corporation to distribute these bonuses among its shareholders, but I would like to see it settled once for all what the money actually expended, under the original contract, amounted to. The day has come when we ought to reduce railway tariffs. The Canadian Pacific Railway can now afford to reduce them and ought to be compelled to do so. The day has come when the Canadian Pacific Railway ought to be compelled to give up these exemptions if it can be made to do so. The day has come when public policy ought no longer to tolerate this company holding its lands in the west and refusing to part with them or refusing to allow settlers to settle on them. Certainly no further privilege should be given it until it abandons that policy. My contention is that both these things are against the public interest and if new concessions are to be given, other concessions on behalf of the public ought to be exacted in return.
I have spoken already three times on this question and have tried to find out what is the feeling of the west with regard to it. So far I have not been able to ascertain that feeling from anybody in this House, but I have read the newspaper opinion in that country, and the oninlon, as voiced by the three newspapers in Winnipeg, is altogether against the Canadian Pacific Railway being allowed to issue its stock at par. The people of the west are of the opinion that as long as they are allowed to do this, the extra tariffs of the company entailed thereby must come out of the people who use the road. If money can be obtained by the company by the sale of low interest bearing securities instead of by the issue of new stock, the company should be compelled to take the former course; or if the company be allowed to issue new capital stock, the market price of that stock should go into its treasury, instead of the advanced price at which it may be sold above par going into the pockets of the shareholders. If that should be done, the amount of capital stock would be kept down, the fixed charges reduced, and that would enable the company to lower its tariff rates. The people of the west and also the people of Ontario and throughout Canada are of the opinion that this practice of issuing new stock at par to the shareholders should not be allowed to continue. If that, however, be not a good practice, let us do away with it. If it be a good pratcice, let us wipe out the right to issue bonds which we now give to railway corporations, and tell the great Canadian Pacific Railway that parliament has no interest in this issue of new stock, as we have been told in this House. That is not the opinion in the United States where the people have a great transportation problem on their hands. Wait until the
fourth of March and see if there will not be a deliverance from the new president of that country to the effect that the day has come when the regulation and control of the capitalization of railway companies is of great importance as bearing on the rates of traffic which these companies may charge. The two questions go together, if you keep down the capitalization and restrict the railway companies to the issue of securities bearing low interest instead of allowing them to issue new capital stock at par, you will be able to reduce their tariff charges in proportion. There is an intimate relation between the two, and therefore I contend that it is the duty of parliament to scrutinize every security issued in connection with our railways in order to see that they shall only issue them on such terms as will secure to the Canadian people, who have to pay the traffic rates, the best possible treatment. We hear a great deal about this company which raises money and does this, that and the other thing for our country. Well, I give it all the credit to which it is entitled. I have no antagonism to these great companies, but I do raise my voice against the man who uses these railways being charged a cent more for that use than he ought to pay. And you cannot keep the tariff rate down unless you keep the capitalization down for the benefit of those who use the road. I shall leave the companies here for the present. I have extended my argument somewhat further than I did on the two occasions I spoke before, and may have a little more to add when we get that other order in council to which I have already referred.
I think I am doing a public duty in standing up here, even if I stand alone, to say that the day has come when we must stop this practice of allowing the great Canadian Pacific Railway Company, at least, to issue securities at par when those securities can be sold on the open market for a premium of almost 75 per cent. It is not in the interest of the public, it is not in the interest of the great Canadian Pacific Railway itself. People say we are turning to socialism in this country, and they denounce socialism and the socialists. But these are the things that are producing this public calamity, if it be a public calamity. To use the words of President Roosevelt, the public ought to get a square deal. I stand here for the square deal for the people of the Canadian west and the Canadian east. I stand here to protest against this distribution of bonus stock amongst the shareholders that is about to take place, and such as has taken place in the past. I want to see this stopped once and for all. And, if I succeed in this, I shall have justified my presence in this House.

The question brought up by the hon. member

for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is, in my judgment, the most important question that will be discussed in this House during the present session. At all events, so far as the western prairie provinces are concerned, there will be nothing discussed here that will be of equal interest to the people. While we want lower duties when we can get them, the question of duties and tariffs fades into insignificance as compared with the question of freight rates, so far as the people of the west are concerned. Representing, as I do, a large, old-settled, well-populated district in the province of Saskatchewan, all clear, open prairie, where a great deal of wheat is produced and where many of the settlers are a long distance from a railway, I may be excused for taking up a small portion of the time of the House in discussing this matter. When the question was brought up some time ago and publicly discussed, different reasons were advanced why this order in council should have been passed authorizing the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company to increase their capital stock by the issue of $50,000,000. One reason given us was that it was the best managed railroad on the face of the earth. Another was that it was necessary to keep the credit of the railway company in good standing. Another was that if the company made a further issue of bonds it would have a bad effect, probably, on the stock that has already been issued, and holders of that stock might find that it was not worth so much. Let us look for a moment at these reasons to see whether they justify in any respect the course that is proposed. Nobody was objecting to the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think it is a fairly well managed company, taking it all round. I do not think its management is ideal; in some respects, in my opinion, it is anything but well managed. If the other companies are all worse managed than the Canadian Pacific Railway, then I can only say God help the others. Take, for a moment, the question of building branch lines. I do not want to be understood as making any attack on the Canadian Pacific Railway in particular, for the Canadian Northern is just as bad, and the Grand Trunk Pacific, I expect, when they are a little older, will get on to the ropes and will do as the others have done. I am not saying that there is any choice in that respect. But what do the Canadian Pacific do about the building of branch lines? Do they consult the interests of the people of the country? No, they consult their own interest only, and that not in relation to the earning of dividends, but with a view to cutting out their opponents. While the people may be suffering fifty miles from a railway, they will build a line within five or ten miles of an existing road, where they think they can cut out traffic from the Canadian Northern Mr. TURRIFF.
or the Grand Trunk Pacific. In that respect, I say, the Canadian Pacific Railway is not a well-managed line. If, as has been said, we are, in a sense, partners in this great railway enterprise, then I think we ought to be given some consideration in deciding where these branch lines should be built. In my own constituency, as an example, we have the spectacle of two railroads paralleling each other for eighty miles at one end of my constituency, so that it is almost unsafe for a man to go in there so strong are the objections of the settlers to these railways having been allowed to do that sort of thing; and, in the other end of the district, the farmers are suffering through being forty or fifty miles from the railway and having to draw their wheat for that distance to point of shipment. And I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and to tell the members of this House, that no man can grow wheat at a profit and draw it with horses forty or fifty miles to a market. And there are dozens and hundreds of settlers in that country who, if some remedy is not found, if railways are not compelled to toe the mark better in the future than they have done in the past, will surely pull out of that country. Has this House no responsibility in this matter? I say there is no possibility of this government or this House of parliament divesting itself of its responsibility. In the future we may rail at the railway companies, but we shall not be able to say, if this sort of thing is allowed to go on, that the railway companies are to blame; the blame must be put where it belongs, on the shoulders of this House of Commons. The railway companies of the past have been doing simply what they liked to a very large extent. They have been walking over us. But when they come to this House and want consideration, they should be dealt with at arm's length and made to give concession for concession. The question of the land grant of the Canadian Pacific Railway has been discussed by my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean). Every word he has said on the subject is absolutely true. He could have gone further and still have been within the mark. We have in that country the spectacle of the Canadian Pacific Railway, with millions of acres of land that was given them for nothing as a bonus to build the original Canadian Pacific Railway, ready to sell that land at a moderate price where it is tributary to their own lines, but, where it is tributary to the Grand Trunk Pacific, assuming a wholly different attitude. And, remember, the Grand Trunk Pacific is being financed by this country, by this parliament-
And queered in London by the Canadian Pacific.

We are helping all the way through, and the Canadian Pacific

Railway is holding them up, playing the dog in the manger, retarding the development of the western country and injuring the credit of Canada just as much as if the country owned the Grand Trunk. Have they any right to do that? I say that it is the duty of the government and of this House, when the Canadian Pacific Railway come here for special permission legislation, as they have done in this case, to say to them:	If we grant you the privilege you
are asking, you must give us privileges in return. And what better opportunity could there be to say to the Canadian Pacific Railway:	'Give up your right to
exemption for twenty years.' If it were not for that right of exemption do you think the Canadian Pacific Railway would put a flat price of $25 an acre on their lands, or, in some cases, withdraw it altogether from the market?-simply because by settling that land it would give trade to the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern. Do you think they would dare to do that? Do you think they could afford to do that? If the school districts and municipalities were able to get at them and tax their land at the same value and at the same rate as the farmers tax themselves, that land would be put on the market, to come under cultivation; the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern would get traffic, and the people would go in and settle on these lands. They do not do it. Not only do they hold that land up, but they also hold the homestead lands up, because men will not go into a part of a country where the odd sections cannot be brought under cultivation and settled on, for the simple reason that they cannot have as good facilities for organizing school districts and giving their children an education as they can in other parts of the country where the odd sections are available for purchase, as they ought to be, and at a fair price. So this is a golden opportunity to say to them: Put that land on the market at a fair price, or at all events, give back your right of exemption from taxation for the balance of the twenty years. If they do that, the rest will follow.
Now as to the argument that their credit would suffer if they sold some additional bonds. Well, I think that any one who advances that argument has not looked very closely into what the Canadian Pacific Railway has been doing of late. Why, only last week I saw an advertisement in the paper that they were paying half yearly dividends of per cent, 7 per cent per annum. They were paying all the fixed charges, paying everything that should be paid, paying a dividend at the rate of 7 per cent per annum, and in addition they would put to the credit of their rest account, for the six months only, over $4,880,000-enough money to have paid dividends at the rate of 12 per cent. The
Canadian Pacific Railway could to-day, out of their earnings, pay 10 per cent per annum on their stock, pay 12 per cent on their common stock, after paying all fixed charges, and still have a reasonable sum to augment their account. Is that not doing well enough? But it is said that by issuing bonds they would reduce the value of the present stock. _ Carry that argument to its logical conclusion, and what does it mean? It means that the Canadian Pacific Railway, who can borrow its money at 4 per cent at the highest, cannot put that money into branch lines in the prairie country- because the reason is given that this stock is issued more particularly to build branch lines in the western country-it means that they could not put that money into branch lines in the west and earn 4 per cent on the cost of these lines. A more absurd statement could not be made. They can earn 4 per cent, and double 4 per cent by building branch lines, if they would build them where they ought to go in reference to the needs of the country and where they would _ get the most traffic, if they chose to eliminate from their ideas the building of branch lines to cut out opposing railways. Sir, I do not think that the reasons given for allowing them to sell this stock at par are good reasons.
It might be well for a moment to consider what the Canadian Pacific Railway got originally. They got $37,000,000 worth of completed road handed over to them; they got 25,000,000 acres of land handed over to them; they got no less than six or seven million acres of land in connection with the charters for the branch lines that they purchased; and they got $25,000,000 in cash as well. So when you come to consider the capital on which they had to earn, you must bear in mind that they did not put all the money into that railway that built it; this country put in a great part of it. Therefore, why, on an occasion of this kind, when they are coming for special favours that they cannot get without the authority of this parliament, why should they not be made to toe the mark and do the decent thing for once? When the original orders in council that my hon. friend read to-day were passed, and it was stipulated that they should not sell their stock at less than par, stock was not selling at 175 to 200 in those days. Why should they be allowed to sell that stock at par to-day to their shareholders? Here is one thing that follows, to my mind: The Canadian Pacific Railway do not want to pay over in cash the immense dividends that they are earning to their subscribers. Why? Because the moment they do that, the people of this country would understand the question a great deal better than they understand it now, and there would be such a howl and a kick put up from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that they

would be forced to reduce their freight rates and their passenger rates. Therefore they take this method, as my hon. friend has pointed out, to divide up $9,000,000 a year in an extra bonus over and above the 7 per cent per annum that is paid on their stock. And remember, Mr. Speaker, that a great deal of that stock on which the 7 per cent is paid, was sold to the men originally connected with it, at. 25 cents on the dollar; so that in the years past they have been drawing 24 per cent to 28 per cent on their money not 7 per cent; and their stock to-day is worth several hundred per cent higher than when it was when they bought it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, don't you think that is doing well enough? Don't you think that is fair enough? Don't you think they have got enough. Why should we turn to now and hand them over between $25,000,000 and $30,000,000 to be divided up among their shareholders? Because, though you may argue it this way and argue it that way, the fact remains that you cannot argue away, that when you issue that stock the people of this country who pay passenger rates and freight rates, one way or another, have to pay and provide the dividends to pay for that stock, the proceeds of which do not go into the coffers of the company, but go directly into the pockets of the shareholders, and the 'people of this country will be compelled to pay extortionate rates to pay these extra dividends that should not be paid at all, and do not need to be paid. Why should this $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 be taken out of the funds of the company? Why should it not go into the treasury of the company? Think what this extra $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 would do. It would build 1,250 to 1,500 miles of railway in those prairie provinces; it would equip those lines thoroughly well, and at the same time would earn dividends to a legitimate extent for the shareholders. Therefore, why should the money be surreptitiously taken out of the funds of the company and put directly into the pockets of the shareholders?
We have heard a good deal in the past about the Jim Hill system. It is very close to us up there in my constituency. The Hill system comes up to within a couple of miles of the boundary. What is the result, Mr. Speaker? Thousands and hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat every year are drawn across the boundary line and sold in the American cities. Do you imagine, or does any one in this House imagine, for a moment that when a farmer goes across into the United States and sells his wheat and gets the money for it, he does not buy his goods there to a large extent? If you imagine that, you are mistaken. They do it every day of the week. From one little town of "Mr. TURRIFF.
700 or 800 inhabitants in my constituency, last fall 150,000 bushels of wheat tributary to that town went down into the United States; and the merchants lost the traffic, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company lost the freight hauling, and the country lost the business. Why? Because the Canadian Pacific . Railway has another charter there that they have held the last seven or eight years; and when I tried my utmost two or three years ago to have a clause put in their charter compelling them to build 25 miles each year, I was not listened to.
They have not built the road, and I do not believe they will until it suits them unless they are compelled to. In the meantime the country is losing the traffic and the business, which is going down into the United States. If this sort of thing continues every man in the country will welcome an extension of the Hill system all through the country, even if it involves the diversion of traffic through the United States rather than longer tolerate the existing conditions. I do not agree with the hon. mem ber for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) in his advocacy of government ownership and operation of railroads. I have never agreed with that; I believe that any company that is running a road in Canada can do it better than this or any other government. I believe the railroads of this country should be built and operated by com panies. But I want to warn the Canadian Pacific Railway and other railway companies and the government and this House that if there is no better control over the railroad companies in future than we now have the people of Canada will be driven to government ownership and operation.
Hear, hear.

I think it would be a mistake, but something has got to be done, and here is an opportunity such as we may not have again. It would be well worth the while of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to go over this matter again, to look into it very closely and to find out what the people of the country think about it. If the people of Canada understood this question, no parliament would dare to give the Canadian Pacific Railway authority to issue that stock at par. The trouble is the people do not understand it, they do not understand what bonuses, what dividends are being drawn by the holders of the Canadian Pacific Railway stock. If they did there would be a change. The minister should thoroughly examine the whole situation and see if something cannot be done to improve the existing conditions.
Let us consider what we might get if the $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 did not go directly into the shareholders' pockets, but

went where they should go, directly into the funds of the company.
First, we might get a lower rate of freight all around.
Hear, hear.

The railroads could cut their freight rates 25 per cent all round if they had this $25,000,000 to use for the benefit and interests of the country.
Second, we might get a lower passenger rate. I had some little part, some two or three years ago, in securing a reduction in railway passenger rates; we succeeded in having the rates reduced from 4 cents and 3i cents to a flat rate of 3 cents per mile on every mile of railroad from the Rockies east to the Atlantic. What was the argument of the Railway Commission? That in some cases higher rates possibly were necessary. We have a Railway Commission who deal with these matters; they are doing first-rate work, and we are giving them plenty of work to do, but there is one point we should not forget, that we cannot shelve all our responsibility on that Railway Commission. This Commission will not take into consideration many subjects that we have to deal with in this parliament, they will take matters as they come before them, and, as a rule, they do not go over the country and order this or that railway to lower its rates. What they do is to take up any matter of complaint that comes before them. There may be one hundred cases of overcharging of freight rates for one that is brought to the notice of the Railway Commission. We have a good commission; it has its work to do; it is doing its work and doing it well, but we cannot divest ourselves of our authority and our responsibility in this matter.
Third, we might obtain the abolition of the exemption from taxation of lands held by the railway. If their lands were not exempted it would not matter what price they put upon them, they would have to sell them, because the higher price they put on the land the more they would be taxed by municipalities or school districts.
Fourth, we might secure the right to say where they will build roads instead of leaving them the discretion they now have.
Fifth, the $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 would rid the country from one end to the other of the deadly level-crossings of which we have heard a great deal.
Hear, hear.

Why should we not make them do it? I say it is up to the House to make these railway companies treat the public fairly.	The Canadian
Pacific Railway is not the only sinner; in many respects the Canadian Northern is a great deal worse, and I intend to take a turn at them later on, but
at present we are dealing with this company, which is no worse than others. I do not think that under any circumstances a company situated like the Canadian Pacific Railway should be allowed to issue stock at par. Would any railway company in the old country situated as this sell their stock at par?
The directors would go to jail if they did.

They would not dare. Look at our banks. They sell their stock at market value and put all the money into the treasury. That is all we ask these people to do. Is it any hardship to compel them to put their money into their own treasury and expend it in building their roads ?_ It must be remembered that while Canadian Pacific Railway is to-day selling at from $173 to $175 it is intrinsically worth at least $200, and the man who has 300 shares and is awarded 100 shares of new stock is in reality getting 100 per cent of a bonus on the stock he holds-and we are the people who are allowing this to be done.
These are some of the reasons why I agree absolutely with what the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has said- and in voicing these sentiments I have the absolute certainty that I voice exactly the sentiments of 100 per cent of the 40,000 people whom I represent in this House- there is no exception. So I say it is up to this government and parliament to do something to bring about a better state of affairs. If they do not take some action they will be taking the very best course in the world to force the people of this country to go in for government ownership and operation of railways.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As some of the questions which have been under discussion are matters with which I have some acquaintance, I may be permitted to make some explanations in respect to them in the hope that those who are interested in these questions, at all events in this House, will have an opportunity of knowing more accurately what the facts are.
I ought to premise, I suppose, that I do not consider myself any defender of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; I do not speak in that capacity at all. I am not financially interested in any way in the undertakings of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; I do not consider that I or my political friends owe that company anything politically. I am one of those who think that the bargain which was made with that company, as contained in our statute-books, was a bargain so advantageous to the company and so disadvantageous to the Dominion of Canada that it ought not to have been entered into. But while I say that, I think none the less that

a contract is so sacred a thing that those who have the advantage of a good bargain are entitled to that advantage and entitled to have that contract carried out in its entirety and according to its true intent and meaning.
The question of authorizing an increase of the capital stock of this company is presented for consideration. Now, the question whether that increase ought to be sanctioned, whether the increase of money which the company is hoping to raise by this means is money that the company needs; and the question of what disposition is to be made by the company of the new stock in order to raise the funds they want, are two entirely different questions, and ought not to be confused. With regard to the first question, which was presented to the Governor in Council for consideration when the company came applying for sanction to its proposed increase of stock, I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) who opened this discussion would not contend that there was anything wrong, illegitimate, against honesty or good morals, in the company if it needed $50,000,000 more of money for its lawful undertakings and for carrying on its operations in this country, proceeding to obtain that money by means of increasing its capital stock and disposing of that capital stock in open market. That is a fair, a proper, a legitimate way by which any company may raise additional capital if it needs additional capital. And in this case, although the capital which the company already had reached the enormous amount of $150,000,000, the very needs of the country which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) who has just taken his seat has so eloquently discussed, demonstrate the propriety of putting that company into a position where if by an increase of its capital stock it can obtain the necessary additional funds it needs, it certainly should not be prevented from doing so by tjhe government of the country refusing its sanction to the desired increase. The increase of the capital stock which was asked seemed to be needed in the interest of the country quite as much as in the interest of the company, and the purpose for which the money to be raised by this increase of capital was to be required was a legitimate and laudable pur-puose, viz., the extension of the company's lines, the constructing of new branches and of new works, betterments in every way, to increase the facility with which the company can do its work of transportation. Every object for which this additional capital was needed was a legitimate and a laudable object in regard to which if there had been obstruction thrown in the way of the company it would have been a step which the parliament of this country would have condemned rather than have approved. If I understand correctly the newspaper discussions which are taking place in certain parts of the country on this question and Mr. AYLESWORTH.
the objection which is being brought forward by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), the only thing of which complaint is made in regard to the increase of the capital is the disposition which the company proposes to make of the additional number of shares by distributing those shares among their shareholders at a figure less than the present market price of Canadian Pacific Railway stock as bought or sold by the public. Now, that is a question in regard to which it seems to me unnecessary that I should express any opinion one way or the other. I shall not discuss it beyond stating this:	That no device of this
nature which a company can apply to its financial affairs will enable that company to increase the amount of its wealth. It has a certain amount _ of property before the increase of the capital stock, and it has that same property in specie, in railway real estate, or in whatever shape you please after the increase of its capital stock. Before the last increase the capital stock of the company amounted to $150,000,000; there were so many shareholders of the company, each holding his share of $100 par value, and the proposition is to increase the capital stock of the company to $200,000,000 and to increase correspondingly the number of shares. _ It is the property of the company which it had before the increase that_ is represented by the number of shares which existed before the increase, and it is that same property plus whatever is paid for the new shares which the company has after the increase, and the company is neither richer nor poorer after the increase except by _ the amount which it receives for the additional number of shares. Now, take the position of any individual shareholder; he receives of course a benefit if he is permitted to purchase for every three shares which he held before the increase one share of the new issue at any figure less than the market price. Assuming that the value in the market of Canadian Pacific Railway shares before the increase was $170, every three shares would be worth, to buy or sell, $510. If a man bought three shares, paying out $510 for his three shares and then being entitled to one new share for $100 paid his $100, he would have become possessed of four shares for $610, and the four shares would have cost him $152.50 each. That measures exactly the extent of any benefit which this proposition of issuing one new share at par to each holder of three shares, gives to that shareholder; he makes $52.50 on the purchase of his new shares if the market price before the increase was $170. The shares of the company decrease in value immediately upon the issue of new stock being put upon the market and decrease in value exactly in proportion to the number of new shares which it issues, and the property which

these shares represent has not been made either more or less by the transaction. So that what we have as a result of this transaction to the individual shareholder comes simply down to this: that each owner of three shares, if the capital stock was worth $170 in the market, has made on his three shares $52.50 by the transaction, or in other words, he has got a special dividend of seventeen and a half per cent. Well now, if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or if any company, instead of adopting that means of giving to each one of its shareholders a special dividend of seventeen and a half per cent had had the funds to distribute among its shareholders, had had the property in money or in money's worth, and had chosen to declare a special dividend to that amount, I do not suppose the newspaper editors of the country would have thought there was any such highly immoral or improper transaction as that which in this other shape the railway company is proposing to enter into and which is now being so vigorously denounced. If any company is in a position, if it has made money so that it is able by its operations to pay a special dividend of seventeen and a half per cent and it does it, it is simply a distribution of the assets of the company in which the public as a whole is in no manner or way concerned.
Now, that is as I understand it the position of any ordinary trading company, any company incorporated for the purpose of gain. If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or any other company operating or enjoying a public franchise is by that circumstance under an obligation to the public which precludes it from taking a course it otherwise might wish to take with regard to its shareholders, that is an entirely different story. If the bargain which this company made with the country, when it undertook to build this railway, has so bound its hands that by reason of the privileges which it then obtained and which it still enjoys from the people of Canada, it is not in a position to deal with its shareholders as a company which was free from such obligations might see fit to deal with them, that is an entirely different story, and the whole question of the morality or the immorality from a business point of view of what is proposed seems to me to bring itself down simply to the question whether or not the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is living up to its contract. If it is, then I cannot see how any man in this country has any right whatever to complain of the course the company is taking. If it is not, then it ought to be compelled to do so. I fully agree with any view which my hon. friend may express or which any other member of this House may hold, that if the company is not carrying out its obligations to Canada it ought/ to be made to do so In this regard let us remember for a moment just what the measure of its obli-43
gation is. It is a bargain; it is a contract which parliament in 1881 sanctioned. It was debated enough at that time, it was entered into by the country with the eyes of the country wide open, and this is the letter of its terms-the general Railway Act at that time provided that no railway company might earn, one might say, more than 15 per cent upon its capital cost of construction without being liable to have its rates reduced by the parliament of the country. When the Canadian Pacific Railway presented its contract to parliament that 15 per cent limitation was lowered to 10 per cent and the obligation of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was to that extent so much the more burdensome upon the company. The limit which the parliament of Canada provided by the general Railway Act was altered to such extent that the tolls of the Canadian Pacific Railway should not produce more than 10 per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in the construction of the railway, instead of not less than 15 per cent, as generally provided.
The question, then, which fell to be considered when the company was proposing to increase its capital stock in 1902, was whether or not its revenue produced 10 per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in the construction of the railway. An OTder in council was passed in January, 1902, authorizing the increase oi the company's capital from $65,000,000 to $85,000,000. It was an express stipulation in that order in council that the $20,000,000 extra stock which was then being sanctioned was not to affect the cost of construction of the railway upon which the 10 per cent was to be calculated under the terms of the contract. The interests of the people of this country were safeguarded by the presence in the order in council of that provision, and the $20,000,000 of increase which was then authorized was not to be taken into account one way or the other in fixing the actual amount expended in the construction of the railway for the purpose of calculating the 10 per cent. In the discussion which then took place, the desire was expressed in many quarters that the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada should be taken on the question whether or not the amount of capital actually expended in the construction of the railway had yet reached such a figure as had made the time arrive when the rates of the company were liable to be reduced, and it was thought better that that should be referred to the court. In the January and February of 1904, the matter was placed by the then Minister of Justice in my hands on behalf of the government, and I was engaged for some two or three months in almost daily conference with the late Mr. Christopher Robinson, who was counsel in that matter for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company,



in the effort, which ultimately was successful, to arrange the terms of this reference to the Supreme Court. It was a very troublesome, difficult piece of work. There were a great many considerations to be taken into account, and the outcome was satisfactorily reached only after many propositions and counter propositions; hut ultimately we succeeded in getting to an agreement as to the terms of the reference which was to be made to the| Supreme Court of Canada. The case was entered for hearing at the May, 1904, term of the Supreme Court, and it was ready for argument, and no doubt would have been argued but for an arrangement which as counsel for the government I at that time understood had been entered into with the railway company. This was a piece of litigation upon which, if one were going to enter, it would behoove him to count the time and the cost. It was a case of such magnitude and importance, and such difficulty as well, that certainly it was not to be expected that either party would be content without an appeal to the Judicial Committee. After the principles upon which the accounts between the company and the public were to be taken had been settled by the decisions of the courts, the trouble would begin-the actual taking of the accounts, the actual going to work and determining, before some officer of the court, in the light of the decisions which the courts might have pronounced upon- I was going to say the almost innumerable points involved-upon the dozens of questions which were raised to be considered, what had been up to that time the actual amount expended in the construction of the railway. This would certainly have been the work of years. From the standpoint of the practising lawyer the prospect was certainly a charming one. Here was the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the one side and the Dominion of Canada on the other, engaged upon an inquiry to ascertain what amount of money had actually been expended in the construction of the railway during what was then 25 years or thereabout. That would have been, as I say, undoubtedly the work of years, and it would have been undoubtedly a very expensive operation. The late Mr. Christopher Robinson, the Hon. Edward Blake, and other counsel of distinction in this country were representing the railway company. It would have been something in regard to which there would have required to be a very substantial expenditure of money on the part of the company as well as on the part of the government. Next there is to be considered what would have been the position if the government had succeeded to the full in its contention at the end of a long taking of accounts. If the government, at the end of a long litigation, had succeeded in demonstrating that the revenue of the company amounted to more than 10 per cent on Mr. AYLESWORTH.
the capital actually expended on the construction of the railway, what then? Why, then, the rates would fall to be reduced. If the government failed, if the company showed that it was not making 10 per cent, then of course the government would have lost its case, and would have been out of pocket whatever it had invested in the inquiry. If it succeeded, the full extent of its success would have been to show that it was entitled to have the rates brought down to a figure which would make the income of the company not exceed 10 per cent on the amount actually expended in construction; and if that were the case, how would the actual amount of those rates fall to be settled? We had then not long before established the Board of Railway Commissioners, a board charged with the duty of deciding just such questions of rates in regard to other railway companies, but not having that control over the Canadian Pacific Railway Company which it would have secured if at the end of the litigation I have described the government had succeeded in demonstrating .that the 10 per cent limit was being exceeded, and that the rates of the company would therefore have to be considered by this tribunal. In that position of matters the company came forward to the Minister of Justice of that day, saying: This prospect of litigation is terrifying, and rather than go on with that reference, we propose to leave the case standing entered for argument before the Supreme Court, in a position where it can be resumed at the wish of either party any day; and leaving it standing there as it is, we propose to submit ourselves, for the present at any rate, to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and leave them free to control our rates. That was done. The company has from that day to this gone on allowing its rates to be controlled by the Board of Railway Commissioners, submitting itself to their jurisdiction in regard to its rates in exactly the same way that any other railway company in this country is obliged to submit itself. In the meantime the interests of the country have not suffered in any respect, so far as the litigation in question is concerned. It stands exactly where it did in the month of May five years ago. It is entered for bearing before the Supreme Court. Either party can take it up at any term of that court; and if it be the will of this House that that litigation should be entered upon, it is in no worse position than it was when it stood over in May, 1904. It can be taken up at once exactly where it was dropped and can be pursued to the end. But when it is at an end, when ultimately,, after the expenditure of thousands of dollars and of years of time, the litigation is decided, and if the government prevail in its contention, the position, so far as the company is concerned, will be identical with that

which it occupies now. What object there can be, in those circumstances, in pursuing that litigation, so long as the company continues to submit its operations and tariff to the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners, I am entirely unable to understand.
But one word more with reference to the different increases which have taken place in the capital stock of the company since 1992. Starting with the capital stock of $65,000,000, that was increased by $20,000,000 and then there was another increase of $25,000,000 in 1904. In 1906 there was a further increase of $40,000,000, and in 1908 a final increase of $50,000,000. In each of these three cases an order in council was passed. In the latter two cases 1906 and 1908, the order in council contains exactly, in each instance, the same protecting provision as the order in council of 1902, namely, that the increased capital which the company w as being authorized to expend in the way of construction should not be taken into account, either in favour of the company or against it, in computing the cost of construction upon which the ten per cent profit was to be based. The order of 1904 did not contain that provision, through some inadvertence or lack of attention apparently in the preparation of it. There was at all events the assurance given by the solicitors of the company, that the omission, so far as they were concerned, was entirely due to inadvertence; and I have in my hand a letter from the solicitor of the company, written with authority, he says, in which the company's solicitor undertakes, as he had previously stated to me by word of mouth, that that order in council of July, 1904, should, for all purposes and at all times, be considered as though it did contain the ten per cent clause in the same language as the other three orders.
What is the date of that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is of recent date, but the conversations which preceded it stated exactly the same thing as the letter does. I asked that the assurance should be put in writing and the letter is dated the 15th February inst. There never has been any other position taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway from first to last; and so far as the disposition of the proceeds is concerned, so far as regards what has been done with the various increases of capital from time to time-this statement is given by the president of the company, the accuracy of which we have no reason to doubt-not one penny of the capital authorized in excess of the $65,000,000 is to be taken into question in estimating the cost of construction under the terms of clause 20 of the company's contract with the Dominion government. And although 43!
it goes without saying, (Sir Thomas Shaughnessy adds) that these vast expenditures for increased facilities and greater developments are very great factors in the growth of the company's net revenue.

I have been very much interested in the discussion and particularly in the speech made by the hon. the Minister of Justice. In that speech the minister says that the original bargain between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian government, which has entailed so many hardships on the people of the west, is sacred and that so long as the company carries out faithfully its side of the compact, we have no right to interfere with it. He also assures the House that the ten per cent on the stock is not a hard and fast rule to day, but that the company, in the revision of its rates, has to take the ruling of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That is an assurance which will be very well received by the House and the country at large. But there is one thing on which I would like to have a little light and that is what the Board of Railway Commissioners would consider a fair basis on which to reckon the contract rate. In other words would they not take into consideration the fact that in the extra issues of stock the rate of interest has been materially reduced. I am not saying that it binds them down, as in the original bargain, to ten per cent interest on the stock, but I ask whether, in all fairness, it would not be reasonable to suppose that they would take into consideration tne amount of stock issued and the interest thereon.
Hear, hear.

But if we must leave that out of the question, if the issuance of the extra stock does not interfere in any way with the rates of the company, if competition and the control of the Railway Commissioners are to bring about a better state of affairs, there is one thing which must be evident to everybody. When the Canadian Pacific Railway come to this House, they must be coming for favours; and when they are coming for extra favours, it ought to be the duty of this House, in view of certain hardships that are entailed on the country by the original bargain, to see that these hardships are in some way relieved.
Hear, hear.

If they ask us for one favour and another, if they want us to put them in the position of watering stock to some extent or issuing it at par, then let us curtail some of the enormous advantages they have secured over the public in western Canada. Of all the questions that give rise to the most irritation concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway and its operation to-day-and I have no fault

to find with the Canadian Pacific Railway and its operations, I will go as far in my admiration of the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway as the Minister of -Railways, and admit that it operates as well as and perhaps better than any railway in the world-there are certain conditions in that original contract which our people most resent and which it is the duty of parliament to use every legitimate means to have done away with, and of those things the main one is that the lands of the company may be held by them exempt from taxation.
If I may be pardoned, I will go briefly [DOT]over the history of this arrangement. In 1881, the bargain was made that the lands *of the Canadian Pacific Railway should be selected from a twenty mile belt and should be exempt from taxation for twenty years. But the railway company came back here and asked for additional favours. They did not like the land within the twenty-mile belt and they were given free selection throughout that western country. In my constituency, whose extreme southern boundary is a hundred miles north of the Canadian Pacific Railway, for all practical purposes every odd section was selected by the company. The twenty years of exemption would have expired in 1901. But the Canadian Pacific Railway patented its land only as it was sold. And, in 1901, when the provinces said: Now your exemption has expired, their answer was:	Our
exemption extends from the patenting of the lands twenty years. And they were asked to select their lands. A great portion of that land was not selected until
1906.	Twenty-five years from 1881 and twenty years from 1906 make forty-five years' exemption for which these settlers in the west must pay. I ask any man in this House who is fair-thinking how the people in the older provinces would like it if they had to pay taxes not only every man on his own farm, but on the farm adjoining.
And the Canadian Pacific Railway cutting up melons of nine millions a year.

Apart from that argument, I would ask any hon. member: How would your constituency behave if your people had twice the taxes to pay that they should pay? How would they like it if no improvement was going on on the land adjoining theirs? But that is not all. We have a provincial law in that country that the maximum taxation per acre for school purposes is ten cents. Schools sections are formed, and, though the settlers are struggling with the difficulties of pioneer life, they want their children educated. They form their school section, but the odd sections of land are in The hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Placing on the maximum of taxation they attempt to build the school. They issue debentures, they make short loans for furniture, and they pay their teacher. But the second year comes. Now, their short loans come due, the payment of interest on the debentures comes due, and the teacher's salary is no less than before. I have two instances in my constituency where these people found that, even with the maximum of taxation, they could not possibly support their schools in the second year. I ask any hon. member here: What would your constituency say if they had to close up their school when paying maximum of taxation, leave the building standing idle and no opportunity afforded for the education of their children? Don't you think that this would become a burning question. Don't you think you would make such a noise in this House that the government would have to act? And if the Canadian Pacific Railway came here for a favour, don't you think the first question would be: What are you going to do about that exemption? This question is, in my constituency, a burning question. These lands bear no taxation for roads, but the expense of improvements must be borne in its entirety by the owner of the adjoining land. The settler goes in there. He has no money to buy the land. He tries the best he can to improve the roads, but he gets no help from half the land there. He is increasing the value of the Canadian Pacific Railway land with every improvement he makes, and with his efforts improving the productiveness of the country. Yet he gets no help from the Canadian Pacific Railway.
And they cutting a melon every year.

I say that, when this matter comes up for consideration before the government, it is the duty of the government to ask favour for favour; when the Canadian Pacific Railway ask for one favour, the government should demand a favour in return. If you will take away the exemption, and compel the Canadian Pacific Railway to sell their lands, you will settle one of the most vexing questions with which we have to do. It is said, this bargain is a sacred one, that we cannot set aside the bargain for the company have carried out their side of it. I do not know anything about law, but I will leave it to the judgment of any man here, if, when that bargain was made in 1881, it was not the intention of parliament that that bargain should expire in 1901? I say we are paying taxes for twenty-five years beyond that bargain, and, dear only knows, the bargain was bad enough in the first instance. This bargain is a sacred one; but the duty that we have to perform is also a sacred one. We are here to represent

the people. The company have vested rights, but so have the people. If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company wishes to go^ through certain territory, the laws of this country are such that they can take the land from the man who has the patent for it on giving him a fair price. It seems to me that if this bargain is sacred, we should use every possible endeavour to do away with what is one of the greatest evils of our country, and one that is retarding the settlement of western Canada to-day.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) to say that the bargain was a sacred one, and that the government were compelled by that bargain to authorize all these issues of stock at par when the stock is selling at a higher rate?

I will put my point in one sentence: When the Canadian Pacific Railway comes to us to ask for favours, we should try to relieve the friction points by asking them to grant us the favour of doing away with these restrictions.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, 1 desire to ask the attention of the House for a few moments to certain reports which have come to hand of statements made in the Senate of the United States with regard to the ratification of the Waterways Treaty now under consideration between the two countries. I refer particularly to despatch in the ' Montreal Star ' of 17th instant:
New York, Feb. 17th.-A Washington despatch to the 'Tribune' says: The prospects for the ratification of the Canadian Boundary Waters Treaty at this session of Congress are growing constantly less, and it now seems inevitable that the convention will have to go over until next session. Even then it may be amended.
And further on:
At the hearing which the Committee on Foreign Relations gave to Senator Smith, of Michigan, yesterday, he made a clear-cut argument in support of his contention that the treaty ought to be amended so as to ensure to his state as large a portion of the waters of St. Mary's river as it now enjoys, while his presentation of his contention that the treaty would deprive his state and this country of a part of those waters made considerable impression on the members of the committee.
iSenator Smith maintained that the treaties of Ghent and Paris and the Webster-Ashbur-ton treaty all defined the boundary, and that during all the intervening years it had remained undisputed. He maintained therefore, that the argument made against his contention-that the committee provided for in the pending convention would have power to fix. the boundary-fell to the ground.
He argued further, that the treaty ratified last year did not alter the boundaries, but merely authorized a commission to erect the proper physical monuments. He said that at present two-thirds of the water of the St. Mary's river ran on the Michigan side of the liver, while under the treaty pending the commission would unquestionably divide these waters equally between the United States and Canada. This, he maintained, would be a serious injustice to his state and to the United States.
Following that, we read in the newspapers to-day^ that it is impossible, on account of objections that have been raised by Senator Smith, of Michigan, on these grounds, that the convention treaty can be ratified during this session of Congress, the consequence of which will be that it will have'to go over to another year. Now, I do not desire to enter upon a discussion of the terms of that treaty. Unfortunately, by a mysterious procedure, and one which does not commend* itself either to the Prime Minister or the leader of the opposition, we are practically in the dark in this House with regard to-the terms of the treaty. But this we do. know, that we had an International Waterways Commission, which commission was constituted and endowed with certain functions and powers. It went to work at considerable expense to investigate our water supply and our waterways, the commission being composed of representative gentlemen appointed by both governments. The report of that Waterways Commission was, with regard to the St. Mary's river, that the power from those falls should be divided equally between the two countries. That report has been adopted so far as it could be adopted by this House. That report is fair in every respect, and has been made after examination by the commissioners of all the water supply and the water sheds on both sides of the river.
Now, I desire to urge upon the right hon. gentleman who leads this House that there should be no disturbance of the conditions on the boundary between Canada and the United States, as found to exist by that independent report of a joint commission appointed by both countries, and that the efforts of the hon. senator for Michigan to block the treaty in order to get better terms, to get encroachments on the boundary, to get water franchises of a very valuable nature properly belonging to Canada, found to belong to Canada, known to belong to Canada, conceded to belong to Canada, and vested in Canada by treaty rights for many years, enjoyed and possessed by Canada today-that that hon. gentleman shall not be permitted, by holding up the ratification of that treaty in the United States Senate, to wrest from Canada something which Canada has a right to keep, and which I pro-

test, as a Canadian representative against Canada giving up at all. What is to be the result, I leave it to the right hon. gentleman who leads this House_ to say. I do not know what negotiations, if any, are taking place. But I now rise for the purpose of setting forth the situation and placing it before the government, namely, that the people of Canada, and especially the people who are immediately benefiting by the water supply from the St. Mary's river as well as those benefiting by the supply of the Niagara river, shall not be deprived of their rights, and that the right hon. gentleman shall see to it, in further negotiations, that there is no leverage made by the blocking of that commission to take away from Canada that which belongs to Canada. There was a lamentable incident in connection with one of our treaties with the United States, so far as territorial boundaries were concerned, there was an arrangement whereby, at the last moment, by a lamentable circumstance or coincidence, a portion of that territory which we honestly belived to belong to Canada, was taken away from Canada by measures which we did not approve, and which the people of this country did not approve. I therefore urge upon the right hon. gentleman to keep a watchful eye on the proceedings of the United States, and to see that no leverage, no holdup, is made by any one on the other side of the line in order to wrest from Canada any part of our waterways, or any part of our territory which has been agreed upon and found to be Canada's by right, and that the treaty shall not be varied or changed to our disadvantage by gentlemen in the United States Senate.

I do not think that there is any cause for misapprehension on the part of my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) by reason of what has transpired, so far as we know, in the Senate of the United States. The newspaper reports which I have Been, I believe, are not very accurate, and in those reports two treaties are confounded the one with the other. The treaty which is now before the Senate, the Waterways Treaty, is eminently fair to both countries. The fact that objection is taken to its terms by a senator in the United States Congress, a gentleman interested on the other side of the line, is perhaps evidence that after all the treaty cannot be objectionable to the people of this country. I would not prejudge it at all. There is another treaty which was passed last year, and which referred to the international boundaries, as to which a commission has been appointed to fix, not new boundaries, not to determine new boundaries, but simply to fix the boundaries already existing by treaty, which has now been in existence for forty or fifty years. The commissioners have no power to depart in any way, under that treaty, from what Mr. BOYCE.
has been in existence, and is now in existence; their task is merely to confirm metes and bounds, marking present boundaries, and nothing else. It is premature, I think, to discuss that treaty, or the treaty which is now before the Senate committee. As I understand, it has now been put over to another session. I may say that I have the authority of His Excellency the Governor General 'to state that we are endeavouring to get authority from Great Britain to lay the treaty before parliament as soon as possible.

In the Ontario buildings there are no new items. These votes are simply to carry on to completion buildings regarding which provisions were made in the last parliament. I spoke to the chief Conservative whip and he was good enough to say that he would be able to arrange to save the necessity of giving details as to these different buildings because the officer who prepared the estimates was not quite ready with the details. He asked to have the Toronto buildings stand. I undertake that if any hon. member wants specific information in regard to any building I shall furnish it.
The minister promised to bring down an order in council yesterday.
Yes, I have it here.
If the minister would just read the part setting forth the urgency.

This Is with reference to the fence around the Mint. The clause in question reads:
That the Deputy Master of the Mint has on behalf of the Imperial authorities, called the attention of the Department of Public Works to the absolute necessity for the erection ot a fence around the iMint building, before minting operations are proceeded with. That this was a matter quite unforeseen by the Department of Public Works until the demand of the Imperial authorities was made. It is submitted therefore, that this is a case which may quite reasonably come within the exceptions provided for in the Revised Statutes, chapter 39, section 36 (a) of pressing emergency in which delay would he1 injurious to the public interests, and that the Minister of Public Works may properly dispense with the calling for public tenders.
That the Chief Architect of the Department of Public Works has prepared plans and a specification which were submitted to, and approved by Dr. Bonar, Deputy Master of the Mint, upon which, the contractors for the Mint building, Messrs. Sullivan and Langdon, were asked to give a price.
That is not the one.
Yes, that is the one.
In connection with the addition to the House of Commons the minister spoke of an order in council setting forth some urgency.

Does my hon. friend not remember that he was speaking of the contract given to Contractors Sullivan & Langdon for the fence and guard-house at the Mint. I promised the hon. member for North Toronto to give the order in council.
Was there an order in council for the expenditure in connection with this wing setting forth an emergency?
Only as to one of the elevators in regard to this building. The $44,000 paid to the contractors in that case is made up of different items of work done without an order in council.
Could the minister furnish the committee with a list of Ontario public buildings for which estimates were passed last year, but which do not appear in the present estimate ?

I stated yesterday that by comparing the estimates of this year with the Appropriation Act of last year it will be seen what has been omitted. Then I was asked if I would prepare a statement of the buildings or works in regard to which tenders had been called, but which had also been omitted, and I said I would do that. I have that list here. It is as follows:

Emilie, P.Q., wharf; West Advocate, N.S., wharf; Devil's Island, N.S., wharf extension; Vancouver, dredging; St. AndrS, P. Q., wharf extension; Long Point, P.E.I., breakwater; Providence Bay, wharf; St. Alexis, Ha! Ha! Bay, wharf; Michipicoten, wharf; Vernon, B.C., public building; Tene-cape, N.S., wharf extension.

In the general election held in October the estimates passed at the last session of parliament were used on behalf of government candidates in many counties in Ontario. It was pointed out to the electors that if they supported certain candidates these buildings would be erected and large amounts of money expended in certain counties.
Did I understand my hon. friend to say it was pointed out that if the electors elected certain candidates this would be done?
Yes.

Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to give the name of the gentleman who referring to what had been placed in the estimates made it a
condition that the candidate would be supported?
I do not propose to be put in the witness box by my hon. friend on details, because I could very well put my hon. friend in the witness box and refer to special cases in his own constituency.
In my own constituency there was no promise of any kind or description which was contingent upon the government candidates being supported.

If we wish to broaden out this discussion there is a gentleman sitting within my hearing whose opponent published a list of the amounts of money that were expended in his county and because of that argued that they should return him again to support the government.

That is another matter. My hon. friend said that the promise was made by candidates that if they were returned these works which were provided for in the Appropriation Act would be undertaken, but making it a condition that such and such candidates would be returned. I asked my hon. friend to point to a single instance in which that was done. Then he referred to St. John, and I told him that in no case was any promise or assurance in regard to the carrying on of a public work made contingent on the election of a particular candidate.

My hon. friend will not venture to say that his government did not adopt the policy of using the promise of public works with the electors to induce them to support their candidates. I could give specific instances, if I chose but I shall not. Perhaps the minister would like me to, so that he could instance some county and point out some member of the opposition who objected to it and was anxious to bring the case before parliament. In last year's estimates were found a great number of items for the construction of public buildings and public works; on these no money was expended last year and they have disappeared from the estimates this year. What I want to know from the minister is the cause. Last year the minister told us there was no fear that the revenue of the country would continue to increase, but he now tells us our revenue has decreased and that the government is short of money. I want from the minister a list of the public buildings in Ontario which were provided for in the estimates last year and on which no money was spent and which are not to be proceeded with under thesg estimates.

That will entail some clerical work which I will have done and I will submit the result to the hon. gentleman later. As I have already explained we cannot save eight million dollars unless

we cut off public works here and there and we have done so all over the country without distinguishing between constituencies represented by supporters or opponents of the government. I do not expect that this postponement of public works will last long. The works were provided for last session in good faith and as we deemed they were necessary in the public interest, I shall consider it my duty at the earliest possible moment to have these works reinstated in the Appropriation Act so that they may be proceeded with.
Cornwall Public Building-Alterations to fittings, $1,400.
What are these alterations and who has the contract?
These are for ordinary post office fittings, new steps to the building, &c. The Berlin, Ontario, Hardware Company has the contract.
Is there pressing public necessity for these alterations ?
I would not have undertaken them were it not that the Post Office Department made an urgent request.

In the estimates of iast year there was an item of $5,000 for the erection of a post office at the town of Chesley. I suppose that the same reason that the hon. minister has given for striking out the other items would apply to the striking out of that item.

The same reason would apply, but I may say that we have decided to purchase the site, so that we shall be ready to proceed with the construction of the building as soon as the necessary provision is made.

Did the hon. minister or his department send any official or agent to Chesley during October last for the purpose of purchasing or arranging for the purchase of a site for the proposed post office building?
I gave instructions to the inspector to go there for the purpose qf looking into the question of the site, but just when he went there I do not know.
Then the hon. minister did send an inspector just previous to the election?
That looks suspicious.
A little bit, but things are not always what they seem.

I may say that during the recent election campaign considerable capital was endeavoured to be made for the government candidate out of the fact that the people of the town of Chesley were to receive a new post office building, and the argument was freely used that it would be Mr. PUGSLEY.
suicidal policy on the part of the electors not to elect a supporter of this government, as the result might be that no post office would be built. Now, the result appears to me to show that the parties who advanced that argument must have had good ground for it. I would like to have the assurance of the hon. minister that in striking out the item for the building of a post office at Chesley, he was not influenced in any way by the fact that the riding did not return a supporter of the government?

I can give my hon. friend that assurance in the most positive terms. I may say that in leaving out the public buildings in regard to which tenders had not been called, we drew the line irrespective of whether a supporter of the government or an opponent of the government had been returned.

I would like to call the attention of the minister in a general way to the fact that the people of the inland constituencies of western Ontario, being large purchasers and consumers of imported goods, contribute largely to the revenue of this country, while they receive a very small return in the way of the erection of public buildings. I wish to say to the hon. minister that the town of Chesley is a thriving and progressive town, fast becoming quite a manufacturing centre, and I would like to have his assurance that, as soon as the finances of the country will be in such shape that he can go on and erect public buildings, he will then take up the matter of the Chesley post office, and have it provided for in the estimates at an early date.

I can hardly be expected to give that assurance in respect to individual buildings; but I give it to my hon. friend in general terms, which ought to be satisfactory. I may say that when the gentleman who formerly represented the constituency in which Chesley is situated, urged its claim for a public building, he used the same argument that my hon. friend does now, in regard to its being a thriving and progressive town and it was in consequence of his very strong representations that provision was made for a building in the town of Chesley. The item was put in the estimates in good faith, and it is in exactly the same position as other items which have been held over. But I can assure my hon. friend that as early as possible the buildings provided last year will be proceeded with, including the building in the town of Chesley.
Was the site purchased?
The site has been purchased.
I would like to ask the minister if this work will be gone on with before the next election?

That depends on when the election will take place.
Glencoe-Public Building, $26,000.
Is this a post office?
A public building, including a post office and custom house.
What is the size of Glencoe?
In 1901 the population was betwen 1,000 and 1,100.

It is not any more now; it is going back; and yet we find $26,000 voted for a public building there. Was the promise of this building the reason it gave the government the big majority it did? It looks very much like it. We find that $1,250 was paid for the site, although land is very cheap there. Were any other sites offered?
Yes, there was an opportunity to purchase several others, but this was regarded as the best and the cheapest.
What is the size of the lot?
100 feet by 165. It is a corner lot.
I find that the legal expenses in connection with the purchase amounted to $33.02. Will this finish the building?
This is to finish the building.
Has the contract been let?
Yes.
Is there a tower and a clock to be put on that building? I have it on good authority that these were promised before the election.
Yes, there is to be a small and somewhat pretty tower on the building.
When were the tenders advertised for?
Some time last fell.
In what month?
That is one of the particulars I have not got. The contract was let on the 11th of September. Tenders were called probably a month before that.
Can the minister tell us how many tenders there were?
No, I have not that with me.
Was this the lowest?
This was the lowest.
I would like to know who were the parties who tendered?
I will have that this evening.

In the list of tenders asked for and given by the minister, I did not hear that tenders were invited for the dam at Montreal river. Is it not a fact that tenders were asked for the construction of a dam at Montreal river last fall previous to the election?
That will come _ up on harbours and rivers, when I shall give full details.
Was there a tender for the dam at Latchford?

My hon. friend will find a sum in the estimates for the dam at Latchford.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
