subtopic: EDMONTON AND SLAVE LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY.

speechtext: Mr. WILBERT McINTYRE (Strathcona) moved that the House go into Committee on Private Bills.

subtopic: EDMONTON AND SLAVE LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to say a word about this first-Bill, respecting the Edmonton and Slave Lake Railway Company. I recognize that it will not result in any immediate action being taken; at the same time I want to put distinctly on record the position taken by some of us with respect to Bills of this character. This is a Bill for the renewal of a charter granted many years ago. The first clause provides that it shall have five years for the completion of the railway. I have no objection to their having five years for the completion of the railway, but, in the Railway Committee, I objected to having it so put that they shall have five years in which they may actually do nothing We have a pretty well recognized rule that whenever a company applies for a renewal of a charter, there should be a provision that they shall commence and, within two years, spend at least 15 per cent of the capitalization, and shall complete the road within five years. It was alleged that, in the case of this particular company, something had been expended upon the railway-

subtopic: EDMONTON AND SLAVE LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Over 15 per cent.
Mr. LENNOX-but nothing had been expended for as much as two years. I submit that the fact of expenditure having been made two years ago has no great bearing upon the matter of a renewal of charter, and that we should at least insist upon the ordinary condition that they would expend not less than 15 per cent within two years.

As I say, I recognize that I cannot make this effective at the present time. But 1 enter this as a protest against this measure, and the same step will be taken as to the renewal of a charter considered in this House the other day. The difficulty is that these things are quoted as precedents, and we are compelled very often to abandon the salutary rule which we adopted some time ago.
. Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on Private Bills.

House in committee on Bill (No. 35) to incorporate the Salisbury and Harvey Railroad Company.-Mr. Emmerson.

I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) in charge of the Bill to change the name of it. I understood well why this is called ' Railroad ' company instead of ' Railway ' company, because, they are using the franchise of a company which is extinct by insolvency, and they want to have a difference between the two institutions. But I would point out to the non. gentleman that the word * Railway' in the Railway Act has a special construction put upon it by the interpretation clause, and it is very bad legislation for us to use the word 3 Railroad 3 and expect the courts to determine that it means the same as ' Railway ', when this latter word is given an interpretation which, in certain cases, manifestly, ' Railroad ' does not have I would suggest that it be called the ' Great Salisbury and Harvey Railway Company,' or the ' Eastern Salisbury and Harvey Railway Company,' or anything else you like. The word ' Harvey ' might be omitted, and some other name used. It is important that we should not have the word ' Railroad ' in the Bill.

There is much force in the point taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) and I concur in his views. So strong has been my feeling with respect to the matter that I wrote to the parties in the city of St. John who are interested, and made a suggestion as to a change in the name. I think, under the rules of the House, the title of a Bill can be changed on its third reading. Therefore, I would suggest that we might put the Bill through the committee leaving the question of the name open.
I thought this,was the time to mention it.

Of course, the use of the term ' railway ' is uniform in the stat-Mr. LENNOX.
ute, and the Railway Act is framed and phrased with the idea that all companies of that nature shall be termed ' railway ' companies, and not ' railroad ' companies. It would not be well to have an exception.
I would suggest the striking out of the word ' and ' and the inserting of a hyphen. Make it ' Salisbury-Harvey Railway Company.' That will distinguish it from the old company.

Having submitted the matter to the parties interested, I feel that we ought to give them an opportunity to select the name. From my knowledge of the geography, I would say that a better name would be the ' Salisbury and Hopewell Railway Company,' for these are the two points connected. As a matter of fact, Harvey is not connected with Salisbury by this railway.
There is no object in keeping it in then.

No material object, but the railway as first operated, under legislation of this parliament, went by the name of the ' Salisbury and Harvey Railway.' I think they wish to retain the word ' Salisbury,' and perhaps it would be more agreeable to them to retain the name ' Harvey ' also.
. Mr. LANCASTER. You might call it the ' Great Salisbury and Harvey.'
Mr, EMMERSON. But it is no greater than it was. You could not impress the public with that.

Let it go through committee except as to that point, and remain in the committee for further consideration.
Mr. EMMERSON, I think that would be better.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
subtopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
Possibly we might let this Bill go to committee. I notice that there has been a good deal of comment on it. Hon. gentlemen who have looked

through it will see that it contains several clauses which I think will need a great deal of discussion, possibly we will not be able to pass them. It strikes me from reading the Bill over that they will interfere with our control of Dominion railways. It was an Act passed by the Ontario legislature giving this company some aid, to which certain conditions were put in, and one of the conditions was that the company should endeavour to get a Bill passed by this House confirming the agreement which forms part of the Act. The agreement contains one or two clauses as to rates and another clause as to amalgamation. I am afraid that these clauses of the agreement would conflict with the jurisdiction that we ought to have over our own roads. However, I think it will be well to send it on to the Railway Committee, because there may be some parts of the Bill that we ought to confirm. It is with no desire at all to do anything that would permit the railway company to get out of keeping its agreement, but it is with the sole object that we do nothing in this House to pass any railway that is chartered by ourselves out of our own jurisdiction by confirming an agreement with any other body. I have no objection to its going to the committee. We will prune it down, and if there is anything in it that we can confirm, we will be glad to do so.

speechtext: I think the minister is right in allowing it to go to the committee. But it appears to me that this Bill will have to be confirmed or passed in its entirety, or not at all. It is simply an agreement between the provincial government and the railway company, and there will not arise any question about it on the part of the railway company, because they do not get any money unless they obtain the sanction of this House to this agreement. However, we can discuss all that. There are some advisable provisions in this Bill regarding the carriage of road material for municipalities on certain favourable terms.

House again in Committee of Supply. Glencoe Public Building, $26,000.
['I will leave that for you to judge.\nSome resolutions reported.']
In making the purchase of the site for this building was an agent of the department sent to get options on lots or how was the site purchased .

I cannot tell exactly, but if my hon. friend desires I will get the information. My recollection is that the usual course was pursued, that is we send our representative, a very experienced man, to the town, he looks over the different available sites, gets the prices, makes an

examination of the lots, endeavours to ascertain at what prices they changed hands in recent years, according to his instructions from the department, and makes his report to the department. I think I can assure my hon. friend that that was done in this case.

The minister states that he has abolished the patronage system in his department. Does this apply to advertising for tenders for public works ? I mentioned last year that in calling for tenders for the construction of a post office at St. Marys, Ontario, the department advertised in 33 papers in that section of the province at a cost of $607.35. I pointed out then that the department advertisement was not inserted in the leading newspapers in that section of the province.

No change has been made so far as advertising is concerned. As I said to my hon. friend last year, we are careful to see that ample notice is given so that all likely contractors would have the opportunity of tendering for public works. In asking tenders for smaller contracts, such as furnishing supplies, or erecting buildings costing $2,000 or $3,000, we do not advertise as widely as with respect to important public buildings. We would not go to as much expense as for a more expensive work. We endeavour to select newspapers that have considerable circulation, but I have not yet felt bound to ignore the rule which has prevailed that we give a preference to papers which are friendly to the administration.
The hon. gentleman continues to advertise in newspapers supporting the government and in no others.

Not exactly, there are some exceptions.
. Mr. BLAIN. I have here 33 newspapers containing advertisements for tenders for the work at St. Marys, and I would like my hon. friend to say if any of these are not supporters of the present administration?
You are pretty nearly corect.
You have abolished the patronage system?
Not as to newspapers.

In western Ontario an advertisement goes into 33 different newspapers for tenders for a small work to be done at St. Marys, and the newspaper with altogether the largest circulation in that section of the province, the London ' Free Press,' is not included.
I think the ' Advertiser ' of that city had it.
It has a much less circulation than the London ' Free Press.'
I think the Toronto ' Globe ' had it also.

I think the Toronto * Globe ' would be on the list. A little change in that particular would be in the interest of the public, and I am sure it would be along the line of diminishing the patronage list. Does not the minister think that in this case too much money was spent in advertising for tenders.

The work was not so very small. The cost wss between $25,000 and $30,000. The amount for advertising was considerable, but if we were obliged to insert the advertisement in the opposition papers as well the cost might be double.

What is the need of so large an expenditure for a public building in such a small place as Glencoe, which, I believe, has a population of about one thousand souls? There is equal necessity for the establishment of public buildings in other towns of larger population and of more commercial importance where there are less facilities than in this interesting and no doubt progressive town of Glencoe. For instance, there is the town of Steelton, near Sault Ste. Marie, where there are very many important industrial works, and where the population are now suffering for the want of those public facilities which it is the duty of the minister to supply. The minister said to a representative deputation from Sault Ste. Marie, Steelton and that district that the strongest possible representations had been made in regard to the interests of that place and that it must be taken into the serious consideration of the government. That place has no postal facilities commensurate with the needs of the population. I would therefore ask the minister why he discriminates in this manner and establishes a public building at an expense of $26,000 to serve a small population like this, and leaves a town of wider commercial importance with practically no facility at all notwithstanding the fact that he has admitted publicly that the strongest possible representations have been made as to the necessity for increased accommodation.

After hearing the numerous complaints from the other side of the House, one would suppose that they have all the grievances upon their side. In that regard I think they are entirely wrong.
The minister in his wisdom has seen fit to deny us one or two buildings that are very important and on the whole we are inclined to give the government credit for using good judgment in this matter and trying to keep house within their resources. The town of Dresden has not adequate postal facilities and although an appropriation was made for a post office in that town it was deemed wise to not build one there for the present. The hon. gentleman from

North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) referred to a town in his locality that wants a public building, but I may say that there is a town in my district that has probably contributed more revenue to the Dominion exchequer during the past two years than his little town has contributed since confederation, and we have absolutely no adequate postal accommodation there. I, however, shall feel disposed to press the minister quite as strongly as some of the other hon. gentlemen a little later on, and I hope with success. I express myself as being more than delighted to see that the government are practising a policy of retrenchment, and I hope that when they feel they can spend money generously again, a policy will be pursued that will make appropriations something in keeping with the needs of the various communities, and that the small communities will not get double what they ought to have and the larger ones much more than is necessary.
Did the hon. gentleman plead with the government for retrenchment when he sat in the House last July, as he pleaded to-night ?
Yes.

I am delighted at the remarks of the hon. gentleman from East Kent (Mr. Gordon). Did he not come from a town where they manufacture sugar to such a large extent I would scarcely have expected such a very sweet speech. He has been able to congratulate the minister and to find fault with him at the same time, and he has sat down fully satisfied that he has done justice to his constituency. There is no doubt a very large revenue derived from the town the hon. gentleman lives in [DOT] and when the minister comes to know of that he will no doubt meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman and do it with as much grace as my hon. friend (Mr. Gordon) has shown in the manner of his asking.

I was not speaking jocularly and I would be obliged to the minister if he would give me an answer to my question.
. Mr. PTJGSLEY. We were pressed very strongly to provide a public building for Glencoe. It was represented to us that Glencoe was the centre of a very rich agricultural district, an important railway centre that several industrial concerns have recently located in the town, that the population was increasing, that the post office and customs office was inconvenient and entirely inadequate, and that Glencoe was the headquarters of a company of the Middlesex Light Infantry which had no place to store its arms and accoutrements, and that a room should be provided in the public building for that purpose. We yielded to these representations. The plan's were
prepared shortly after parliament rose last summer, tenders w'ere called for and the contract entered into before we arrived at the conclusion we would have to cut off a great many of these items.
The comract was let just before the election.

It had to be let before the election if it was to be done at all last summer. Just one other word, and I say this for the information of our friends on this side of the House whose feeling has been so well expressed by the hon. gentleman from East Kent (Mr. Gordon). There was an appropriation for a building in the town of Grand Falls in my own province put in the estimates last year on the strong representation of the hon. gentleman who represents that constituency and we have omitted it this year although the constituency of Madawaska and Victoria gave to the government candidate a majority of 1,500. Fairville, in my own constituency, is a very thriving and prosperous town adjoining the city of St. John, and it gave me a splendid majority, but I have dropped the appropriation for it from the estimates also. In the city of St. John I have postponed the building of a drill hall which has been promised for years.
They wont give you a majority next time.

Yes they will, because the people of St. John appreciate our efforts to curtail at the present time and they know we are doing the right thing in the public interest. In Kings and Albert where a victory was won by my hon. friend (Mr. McAlister) which was surprising to a great many of our friends opposite we had an appropriation for the thriving .town of Hillsborough and that has been stricken from this year's estimates also. I mention this to show that we are treating constituencies which returned government supporters in the same way as we are treating those constituencies which returned Conservatives. Last session we provided for a good many public buildings and wharfs throughout the country which we thought were necessary, and for that policy we were criticised by hon. gentlemen opposite very strongly. The lieutenant of the leader of the opposition in the province of Quebec took the ground last year, as he took it only yesterday, that many hon. members apparently come here with the sole idea that they must get a public building for their constituents. I hope that remark will not apply to my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce). The same gentleman told us also that those gentlemen who are asking for public buildings are never found in the committee rooms doing the work which devolves properly on members of this parliament, but that their sole object appeared to be to get

a public building. I trust that remark does not apply to my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce). I take a different view altogether; I believe that gentlemen who represent the great cities of Canada ought to look with a favourable eye upon the efforts of the government to give public buildings costing reasonable sums of money and affording ordinary accommodation to the smaller cities and towns throughout the Dominion. That was the policy which the government recognized in submitting the estimates last session. I can tell my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) that if I remain Minister of Public Works I shall regard the claims of Milton favourably, as I shall regard also the claims of other cities and towns to which my attention has been called. But we cannot do everything at once. We find our revenue is limited this year and we have been forced with great reluctance to curtail expenditure. I have been constrained at the instance of the Minister of Finance to cut off the very large sum of $8,000,000 which I had hoped would be placed in the estimates for the purpose of carrying out the obligations entered into last session of parliament when these appropriations were made. I trust this declaration will be sufficient for our hon. friends and that they will recognize the sincerity of the statement I make again, that so far as I know not one of these items was placed in the estimates last year for the purpose of influencing the electors.
No one would not think of charging that.

We placed the appropriations in the estimates because we believed these works were necessary in the public interest. Will any one of these hon. gentlemen rise in his place and say that any one 'of these public buildings is not reasonably required in the public interest? The most hon. gentlemen opposite do is to say: If you are erecting a building in that town give it to the town I represent. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) whom I am always glad to hear, pleads for a public building in Milton and properly so, and when the time comes, as no doubt it will come, when we can give a public building to Milton my hon. friend will be able to say to his constituents: See what I obtained for you as your representative, send me back again to Ottawa in order that I may get further favours for my town.

I cannot allow these pleasant remarks of the Minister of Public Works to pass without notice. I must congratulate him on the admirable statement he has made with regard to his general policy. It is extremely plausible on its face; it certainly seems to be extremely fair and unbiassed. The difficulty is that when the hon. gentleman comes down to Mr. PUGSLEY.
particulars, he departs entirely from his genera] policy. I agree with him very largely on his general policy; but when he tells this committee that the village of Glencoe, of which I have some knowledge, having been there time and again, is entitled to a public building because it is in the midst of a rich agricultural country,
I ask, what better agricultural country can you find than that surrounding the town of Milton? He says Glencoe is a railway centre. I believe there is one line of railway passing through it, with a spur to another village. But both the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific pass through the town of Milton. He says Glencoe has some industries. So has Milton, some very important industries, and it has recently added others. In the village in which I live, in the same county, there is one industry employing 300 men, and another employing from 100 to 150 persons, and it has a population nearly double that of Glencoe. But these minor considerations, to which the hon. gentleman made reference, do not seem to weigh with him in deciding the location of a public building. The special reasons assigned on behalf of Glencoe are applicable to very many towns throughout the province of Ontario, and I have no doubt to very many towns in other provinces which have received no consideration from the minister. However, in this instance I suppose we shall have to allow the general policy to prevail, because we know that the majority in west Middlesex on the 26th of October was very small indeed.

I have listened in vain for an answer from the minister to the question put by the hon. member for Algo-ma (Mr. Boyce); but while I was listening I was delighted to a certain extent to hear from the minister what we may consider to be a specimen brick of the political virtue of himself and his party. I am learning the business of politics. I find that the proper policy is to make an appropriation immediately before an election ; and when the minister gets a large majority, as he did in certin constituencies in New Brunswick, he tells us with unctuous declamation that he withdraws that appropriation, intending of course to use it again at the next election. I have picked up this little piece of general information as to the political policy of himself and his party, but I have waited in vain for an answer to the very reasonable question put by the hon. member for Algoma : why is Glencoe to be accorded a building at the cost stated, although it has a population of only 1,000, while a place like Steelton, with a population of 3,000, whose claims the minister recognized before the election, is discriminated against? Steelton is entitled to say that the minister is bound to recognize its claim if he

is not distributing the public moneys for the purpose of doing favours instead of advancing the interests of Canada. Why is Algoma not treated as it is entitled to be treated because of the solemn promises and representations made by the minister?
There were no promises.

Strong representations he has made here to-night. I heard him say that he led that delegation to suppose that they had made a good claim. Another place without nearly so good a claim is given a public building. I have heard no answer justifying this discrimination. I have only heard that the public moneys of Canada are being played with by the party opposite for the purpose of its political advancement in the constituencies.

How often has this public building been promised to Glencoe before the election? Is this the third or fourth time? In how many elections before has it been promised?
lie buildings is as follows: Renfrew, $6,919; Parkhill, $3,364; Glencoe, $2,871; Leamington-	Markham, $2,143; Simcoe, $7,-
908; Whitby, 4,320; whereas the town of Parry Sound had a revenue of almost $9,000. Then in the matter of post office orders, I find that the total amount issued by these seven towns, which have been so favoured is $132,000 while those issued by the town of Parry Sound alone amounted to $290,000. I find also that the customs revenue for Parry Sound amounted last year to $53,567, which is much larger than that in any other of the towns for which we have been asked to vote an appropriation. And when this matter is brought before the minister, I would ask him to consider very carefully the claims of this town- a town which has three railways connecting with it and the finest harbour on Georgian bay, and which has been neglected to the present in this respect.
What was the cost of the land?
I am not aware of any.

There is another question. The question of advertising which has been raised by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Plain) is a very serious one. When this matter of advertising arose and the question was asked the minister, why he did not distribute his advertising amongst the papers of both parties, he said with a great show of rectitude that he had abolished the pernicious patronage list. Why does he not follow the example of the Tory government in Toronto, and distribute the advertising among both the Reform and Conservative papers? How can he expect the people of this country to believe his solemn assurance that the patronage list is abolished when any one who picks up a Reform paper and a Conservative paper will see a government advertisement in the one and not in the other? He must necessarily come to the conclusion, if he has any eyes or judgment at all, that this story of the abolition of the patronage list is mere moonshine.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the necessity of providing at the earliest possible moment a public building for the town of Parry Sound. I heard him announce that the policy of the government was to provide for those towns which had a certain population and whose necessities were most pressing. The town of Parry Sound has a population of between 3,000 and 4,000. It is one of the principal ports on the Georgian bay, is a large manufacturing centre, is the county town of the county, and has a large postal revenue. According to last year's returns, the postal revenue of those towns in Ontario which have been favoured with pub-
What was the total of the successful tender?
Geo. A. Proctor, of Sarnia, tendered for $16,228, which was the lowest tender and he was given the contract.
When did the work begin and when is it likely to be completed?
The contractor has to begin in the spring. The contract has been let and the building must be completed the first of October next.

I have no desire to obstruct the hon. gentleman's estimates, but when questions are asked him which are reasonable we are entitled to a satisfactory reply and consideration. The answer he gave the proposition I submitted was most pathetic and unctuous but not all satisfactory. In it he deprecated the lavish expenditure of public money on public buildings, especially just before the elections, and desired that his followers should be more moderate in their aggressive demands on his department. What a contrast to one of his predecessors who, when criticised for his very lavish expenditure replied : ' Wait until you see what we will do next

year.' But after the pathetic appeal of the present minister, one cannot help concluding that it must indicate a decline in the power of this government, since it admits that the means by which it has held power is shrinking in its hands. The minister stated that as our revenue began to decline. so should our expenditure on public works. But he knew that last session. Why did he not then practice that policy? Of course the elections were then at hand. And how is he expending the money he asks us to vote? As a Minister of Public Works, he is bound to see that the expenditures are made where they will do the greatest good to the greatest number; and if any cutting down be necessary, it should be done at the expense of the least important and not of the most important centers. But he has followed the opposite policy. He has starved the important centers and expended immense sums on public works where he thought they would most benefit his party, regardless of the principle I have just expressed and which no one can controvert. He has been extravagant in the smaller places and starved the more important ones. Take for instance the town of Steelton, which is of much greater importance than the town of Glencoe. It has a population three times as large. The capital employed there is 25 to 50 times that invested in Glencoe, and representations were made to the government as to the urgent necessity of a post office in Steelton long before there was any question of building one in Glencoe. Yet we have the minister telling us that although he found it necessary to cut down expenditure because of our declining revenue, and although there was not enough money to go around, he has decided that there must be an appropriation for the town of Glencoe, small as it is, and the claims of Steelton are to be utterly disregarded. What can be the reason? How is it that we find this utterly unjustifiable discrimination made by a minister who tells us he has abolished the patronage list? The reason is no doubt that the county of West Middlesex has elected a supporter of the government for two or three _ parliaments and is expected by the minister to do so for still another parliamentary term. What the minister was looking to was political expediency and his object was to expend the public money where it would benefit his party most, regardless of public necessity. Consequently what the hon. minister thought was a reasonable demand on the part of the town of Steelton before the 8th of June last, he now utterly ignores, and finds it necessary instead to benefit the town of Glencoe, and in this way help his supporter, the hon. member for West Middlesex, to keep his seat.	.
Now, I wish to say to the Minister of Public Works that his unctuous utterances Mr. BOYCE.
with regard to retrenchment will not satisfy the people of Canada that he has done, or is endeavouring to do, that which is absolutely square in the expenditure of these appropriations. Where he does see the necessity for retrenchment-where he finds his government crippled by a falling revenue-he must see that the only way to win the public confidence is to show the people that he is capable of presiding oyer his great department with fairness^ and impartiality, which he should exercise absolutely without regard to political exigencies, and taking account only of the public demands and necessities. In that case, the town, irrespective of the political complexion of the member from the district, should receive the expenditure of public money according to the needs of the public service. At the risk of taking up the time of the committee, I think I am entitled to more reasonable and fair answers than the hon. gentleman has so far given. I would like the hon. gentleman to say whether or not he subscribes to the proposition I put. that, when he finds himself in the pathetic position in which he is, and in which he has asked for the sympathy of the House and of the whole country-the position of not being able to supply all the public works he led the people to expect-does he not think that he should supply first those of greater necessity? And let him then say, if he can, having regard not only to his utterances, but to his correspondence, that he would prefer, from the point of view of the public convenience, public interest a.nd public demand, to give that appropriation to the village of Glencoe instead of to the town of Steelton.
Stripping his question of verbiage, will the hon. gentleman be good enough to repeat it?

Apparently, from being unctuous, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugs-ley) thinks he can get over the question by being jocular. I have stated my proposition three times. But perhaps he wants time to think over his answer. I ask the hon. gentleman this: Whether, when, as he has stated, he is called upon to retrench and as he calls upon the members who follow him to accept retrenchment, he does not think he should make curtailments where expenditures are less needed in the public interest rather than where they are more needed in the public interest?

I am glad to answer the hon. gentleman's question. I think he refers to certain representations which were made to me with regard to the town of Steelton. First, I made no promise to the representatives of the town of Steelton that I would place in the estimates, an amount for a public building there. They made very strong' representations to me.
That is not answering my question.
I wish to explain this before proceeding further.

Would my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) pardon me if I interrupt? Does he mean to say that he never made representations that there would be an amount in the estimates for the construction of a public building at Steelton?
If the hon. gentleman says I made such representations, no doubt he is correct. I would like him to produce the letter-does he say they were made in a letter?
I have asked the hon. gentleman a question.

I do not recall at present having made such representations. If my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) says I did make them, I should feel bound to accept his statement as a member of this House. All that I can recall to mind with regard to Steelton is that I was waited upon by certain gentlemen who urged very strongly the claims of the town in regard to better postal accommodation in the erection of a public building. I was much impressed with their claims, and my recollection is that I told these gentlemen that I would take the matter into my careful consideration. I think that is as far as I went. If the hon. gentleman has a letter containing anything stronger I should be obliged if he will produce it. In the last session of parliament a large number of buildings were provided for. The claims of various towns and cities were pressed upon my attention. No doubt Steelton was not provided for because it was felt that we could not ask for further appropriations. No doubt its claim stood over for full consideration later on. I have no doubt that such is the case. Last session we all hoped that the falling off in the public revenues would be but temporary. For my part, I did not dream that there would be such a falling off during the present fiscal year as there has been, that during the eleven months of the present fiscal year there would be a falling off of $10,000,000 or $12,000,000. When, in December last, we were called upon to determine what retrenchments we would bring into effect, as I stated yesterday, and, I think, repeated to-day, we drew the line sharply between those public works in regard to which tenders had not been called for and those in regard to which tenders had been called for before this decision was arrived at. Glencoe was one of those in which tenders had been called for. Parliament had voted the money, and it was up to me to proceed according to the authority of parliament and engage in the work. I could not, in December last, choose 44
as between Steelton and Glencoe, because there was no appropriation for a public building at Steelton. I think that is the best answer I can give my hon. friend, further than to say that, as a general rule, there is no doubt that the cities and towns having a larger population are more entitled to public buildings than those of a small population. But that rule cannot always prevail. In some towns and cities considerable federal expenditures have been made for other purposes than public buildings. It may be that wharfs have been constructed, or harbours have been dredged. In others the construction of a public building would involve the only federal expenditure likely to be made there. As a general proposition, the larger towns are entitled to the first consideration. But it must be borne in mind also that the places in regard to which appropriations were made were pressed very strongly upon my attention by the members of parliament. They came to confer with me and to present the claims of the towns situated in their constituencies. I cannot recall that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) pressed the claims of Steelton on my attention on more than one occasion. He may have done so, but I do not recollect it. And hon. members on the other side were rather disposed to resent an appropriation for public buildings in different constituencies and to suggest that the construction of a public building was an attempt to bribe the constituency. It may have been-I do not say that I recall that it was-my tender solicitude for my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) that prevented me looking towards his constituency, fearing that it would be represented as an unworthy attempt to bribe his constituency and prevent his election as a member of this House.

Is it the intention of the Minister of Public Works to devote this $8,000,000, which he is retrenching this year from the public expenditure, to the erection of new buildings and new wharfs instead of those that were promised last year?

I made a statement on this subject last evening, perhaps the hon. member was not present. I said that when these estimates were submitted to parliament they were submitted in good faith, and in the belief that these various works which were provided for were necessary in the public interest. In leaving the amounts out of the estimates this year we had not the slightest idea of abandoning those works, but simply of postponing them for a short period. Speaking as a general rule, I would say that the works which were provided for by parliament last session, should I be the Minister of Public Works next session and the revenues are in a good condition, as we expect them to be, I would



regard it as my duty to propose that provision should be made for the various works which were provided for at the last session, but which are not provided for in the estimates of the present session.
Is it the policy of the minister to grant post offices costing about $27,000 to places where the population is only 1,000 or so, as he did in Glencoe?
I hope to get the expenses for public buildings in small towns cut down to a sum considerably below that.

The minister has stated that last December he came to the conclusion that it would be necessary to retrench the expenditure to the extent of some $8,000,000. To-night he has gone a little further and says that it was by reason of certain representations made to him by the Minister of Finance. Now, the Minister of Finance, speaking in July last, said that he expected a continuous fall in the revenue for some time to come, and that for the following year the people would have to face a falling revenue. Therefore, the conditions existed in July, and even prior to July, which would necessitate retrenchment. Now I want to ask the Minister of Public Works whether anything in the nature of a collapse or an accident happened to the finances of this country in the fall or immediately prior to that date in December when this government decided on this retrenchment, or was it simply a continuous fall in the revenue such as was predicted by the Minister of Finance?

I can say to my hon. friend that so far as I am concerned, speaking as the Minister of Public Works, I did not expect so large a falling off in the revenue as has taken place. I hope that the turn has come now.
I asked if anything had taken place in the nature of a collapse or an accident?
I am not aware of it.

The minister will remember that when asked in this House last July where he would procure the money with which to erect all these public buildings that he was dangling before the electors, he made reply that there was no need for concern on that point; his information was to the effect that there was no need at all for concern. In volume 7 of last year's ' Hansard,' page 13330, my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) asked this question:
How does the hon. gentleman propose to get all the money to pay for these public buildings? I notice that the revenue is falling off at the rate of a million a month.
Mr. PUGSLEY-My information is that we need not have any fear on that score; but if Mr. PUGSLEY.
by any accident the money is not available, the work will not go on.
Now the minister assures us that there Ms been no accident, simply the falling off in revenue that was anticipated. In July that same condition of affairs existed, and was pronounced by the Finance Minister as likely to continue for many months to come, so that the country has no reasonable explanation why the retrenchmet was made in December. Now, the attack of the opposition is directed, not so much against the fact that appropriations have been made, or that retrenchment has been adopted, it is against this state of affairs, that two or three months before the elections last year the minister proposed various appropriations of money throughout the country, and led the country to believe that these buildings would actually be erected, and by reason of those appropriations which he dangled before the electors, the government was able to carry the country. The minister assures us now that no intent existed in his mind, or on the part of the government, of carrying constituencies by those means. I wonder with what anguish of soul the minister must have witnessed his own candidates in the last election so utterly and so basely misrepresenting the motives of the government throughout this country when they appealed to the electors to vote for the candidates of the government because of these very appropriations that had been promised. Will the minister deny that either he or other ministers of the crown stood on platforms in this country and faced wide streamers requesting electors to vote for the Liberal candidate and a post office?
I never heard of such a thing.
The minister could not hear the streamers but he might see them.
I never saw them.

Will the minister deny that some of his colleagues in the cabinet did not speak in the presence of streamers of that kind, without protest and without correction and without any effort on their part to represent those pure motives of the government so innocently portrayed by the Minister of Public Works to-night. It may possibly be that the government has acted fairly between the parties in the matter of appropriations for buildings that have been gone on with and those which have not, but the minister knows and the country knows that the government very discretely allowed two months to elapse between the date of the elections and the date of this determination, so that they had two whole months within which to adjust the bounty of the government to met the exigencies arising from the vote of October

26. In the third place, I would ask the minister to submit to the committee a list of the advertisements that were published for the first time between the 26th of October and the present date.
I shall be very glad to do so.
Do I understand that the minister will not answer my other two propositions ?
I have answered them.

If the minister thinks that he has said anything which would lead one who desires frankness, to think that he has reconciled his reply to the hon. member for Peel on July 16, 1908, with his statement to the House to-night, I am afraid he is greatly mistaken. It will not satisfy me.
I am very sorry.
If the minister would be kind enough to come to my constituency next election I will show him it will not satisfy the people there.
We have heard something similar to that before.
The minister declines to answer my first two propositions.
I don't want to be discourteous to the hon. gentleman but I have answered them.
No one on this side of the House complains of the discourtesy of the minister.
Do you mean to complain of my want of courtesy.

Not at all, but we are
gradually coming to the conclusion that the minister is a very astute politician.
Is that a compliment or otherwise.

I understand that the minister will bring down a list of all the advertisements that were actually published after the 26th of October, with the amount opposite each one of the appropriations for this year.

I shall be very glad to do so.
Kingston-Royal Military College-Additional accommodation, $57,000.
What is that for ?
Quarters for the subordinate staff.
The departmental report of the minister says " Servants Quarters." Here, the government has built sixteen, five room cottages at a cost of $77,000. Is not that extravagant P 441

Public tenders were called and the work was awarded to the lowest tender. I cannot believe that the price was excessive because the competition was quite keen. I think there are more than five rooms in each dwelling.

Your own departmental report says there are five rooms in each dwelling. These servants who are drawing from seventy-five cents to $1.25 per day are supplied with houses worth $5,000 or $6,000. There are a great many workingmen in this country who would like to be treated as well as that.

I am free to say that I never was thoroughly satisfied that the expenditure for these buildings ought to have been so large as it is, but the plans and specifications were prepared before I became Minister of Public Works. The requisition was made upon us by the Militia Department for these quarters. They are not for what might be called servants but for the subordinate staff; the instructors and teachers in connection with the military college and school. The plans do provide for quite nice dwelling houses, and I am rather inclined to think that it would have been better had plans of a more simple design been prepared. I cannot but believe that the cost of these buildings built as they are is reasonable. I remember I had some hesitation in regard to the matter and I provided that half of them should be erected last year and half during the present (year. There is no way to get out of it; the buildings are completed and this amount is to pay the balance. It may be, as I have said, that if the design of the buildings had been more simple, a few thousand dollars might have been saved; but we have good apartments for the staff, the buildings are substantially constructed, and we have received good value for what we have paid.

If my hon. friend will allow me, I will read the description of these buildings in the report of the Department of Public Works, at page 22:
On January 15, 1908, a contract was entered into for the construction of two buildings, each 167 feet long by 33 feet broad, placed on two opposite sides of a square, facing outwards, with yards in rear; each series separated by a lane which bisects the square.
Each block consists of eight dwellings of two stories in brick with stone dressings and on a stone basement.
The division walls, the partitions in basement, the lining of basement walls and the chimneys are of brick; the partitions, floors and stairs of first and second stories and the roof are of wood; the floor of basement and verandahs in rear are of concrete, and the front entrance steps are of stone.
Each dwelling has, in basement, a cellar, a laundry and a store-room; on the ground floor a living room, a kitchen, an entrance hall, a vestibule, a stairway hall and a verandah,

and, on the first floor, two bed-rooms and bath-room.
These are the rooms of an ordinary everyday ,five-roomed or six-roomed cottage, which could have been built, I should judge, from my knowledge of building, for about $1,500 apiece; and yet we find that the minister has paid the sum of $55,000 last year and $57,000 this year for these paltry terraces' If there were modern fortifications hidden away in the basement, or something of that kind, we could understand the item; but no one who knows anything about the ordinary building trade would justify such an enormous expenditure for two small blocks of five-roomed cottages. I would like to have some more satisfactory explanation of this.

All I can say to my hon. friend is that the requisition was made by the Militia Department and that plans were prepared by the chief architect's department. When my hon. friend says that these buildings could be erected at a cost of $1,500 for each dwelling, my answer is a perfect answer-that tenders were called for by public advertisement widely circulated in the various newspapers, that four tenders were received, and that the lowest was $77,939 and the highest $85,000, for sixteen dwellings in two terraces, eight dwellings in each.
TxiYLOR. Why do you ask for $112,000 if the building^ cost only $77,000?
That is for the buildings alone. Heating, boilers, electric wiring, fixtures, furnishings, sidewalks, &c., are in addition.

I think the hon. minister might gracefully accede to our request to let the item stand, and bring down the plans and tenders. I supposed, from the statement of the minister as to the cost of these buildings, that they must have been trimmed inside with marble, the walls frescoed, and supplied with electric chandeliers and all modern improvements; but now I find that the improvements are extra.
I have no objection at all to bringing down the plans and specifications and the tenders for the information of the committee. The item may stand.
May I ask where these sixteen servants were housed before?
They are members of the subordinate staff, part of the permanent force. They were in Toronto, and were brought from there to Kingston, as I am informed.
I live in Toronto and have a knowledge of military matters there, and I never heard anything of that kind in regard to the Toronto garrison.
I think that was the statement of the Minister of Militia last year.
Why should the servants be in Toronto while those they were serving were in Kingston?
I presume they must have been doing the work in Toronto.

I am glad to find the hon. minister so candid and frank in stating his policy, and I am glad that that policy is that public buildings should only be erected in places where the revenue is overflowing and where such facilities are most urgently required. The reason I say that is because in the district of Nipissing foundations have been laid for five of the greatest cities that we shall perhaps have in the Dominion of Canada and they conform in every respect to the condition stated by the minister in regard to both population and revenue. The first of these young cities is Sudbury. I need not mention its population, because it is increasing every day; but I might mention that it has a suburb with a population of over 3,000 inhabitants and one of the greatest nickel works in the world. Yet Sudbury has not a public building fit for any person to go into. A friend of mine remarked not long ago that he had gone into the post office and could not turn around to come out, but had to back out. The next-young city is Sturgeon Falls, the population of which is probably greater than that of any of the towns to which public buildings have been given to-night, with the exception of the cities. It has a very large water-power and immense paper mills and a fine agricultural country around it. Then, going up to Cobalt, we have there the foundation of one of the largest cities that Canada will perhaps ever see. If the hon. minister has not already been there, and would go up with me and see silver being practically shovelled into cars, he would I am sure come to the conclusion that a place which possesses such wealth should not be left with the insignificant little shanty it has for the people to do their public business in. Going north a little further, we have another young city called Haileybury, which is in the mining country and is doing an immense business, and where the revenue and population are up to the requirements of the minister. Right within three miles, we have the town of New Liskeard, which is also in the same class and in the midst of a very important agricultural country; and I should judge, from the policy the minister tells us he intends following with regard to public buildings, that he will see the propriety of giving to each of these places a suitable public building.

I understand the Minister of Public Works has stated that these

houses will cost $87,000. I notice that a vote was asked last year for $55,000 and that we are now asked to vote another $57,000, making $112,000 for these 16 houses or $7,000 a piece. Is that correct?
That is the estimate now.
Who are to occupy them?
The subordinate staff.
I presume that means the sergeants and officers' servants?
Principally the instructors.
The sergeant-major and sergeants-how many?
Sixteen.

And these subordinate instructors are to have houses built for them at a cost of $7,000 a piece. I call that disgraceful and ridiculous. I am surprised that the Minister of Public Works, after protesting this evening his desire to take the greatest care in expending the public money, should sanction an expenditure of this sort. I am a new member, this is my first session in parliament, and possibly I am more surprised than I will be later on that such utterly absurd and extravagant expenditure should be allowed by any minister of this government.
Kingston-Royal Military College-Barrack accommodation for stables, $15,600.

I would like to point out to the minister that Kingston is a fortress which has existed for years and has accommodation for these men. When the fortress was first built, accommodation was provided for some 3,000 or 4,000 men, and I cannot understand why we should require to spend $15,000 for stables. How many horses will have to be lodged in these stables?
The building is 35 feet by 41 feet and two and a half stories high.
What is the one and a half story on the top floor for?
I cannot say at present. Public tenders were invited and it is expected that $15,000 will be required to pay the balance due on the contract and also for the necessary fittings and furnishings.
How many horses will the stable accommodate?
In the absence of the Minister of Militia, I cannot give the information.
The minister has had the plans and his staff should know. It is he who is asking for the money and not the Minister of Militia.

As I said before recess, I am taking up the Ontario items without having the full details, as the gentleman who prepares them is not quite ready. By the indulgence of the committee I was allowed to go on. I am willing to allow this item to stand and the Kingston veterinary hospital and will later give all the information.	,
Leamington-Public Building, $23,000.
When were representations made as to the necessity for this building?

There was a petition in 1907 urging that there should be a public building there.
Markham-Public Building, $10,000.
When were tenders called for?
The date of the contract is May 20, 1908.
What was the cost of advertising? I see that $633 was the amount voted for advertising in the case at Glencoe.
The total amount of legal expenditure, printing and advertising was $133.21.
What is the population of Markham?
Not at all, it is only about 1,000.
The statement given me says 5,000. It is probably an error of the typewriter.

When were the plans prepared? And is the minister aware that in December, 1907, the plans for that public building were exhibited throughout that constituency by Mr. Archie Campbell, who then represented it? Did he do this by the authority of the Minister of Public Works or on his own responsibility? He had the plans of the post office in 1907.
That might be.
Was that done as a bribe by Mr. Campbell and with the authority of the Minister of Public Works?
I know nothing about it.
What is the total cost of this building?
The original contract for the building was $6,900. Taking the cost of the site, the heating, fittings, including letter-boxes, sidewalks, &c., the total cost was between $15,000 and $16,000.

I have no objection to the expenditure, but only to the way it was

brought about, by Mr. Archie Campbell going into the constituency after he had resigned from this House.
He may have been consulting some of the people
Was he authorized by the minister to go there in December, 1907, with a plan of the building?
Never heard of it.
Is there to be a clock in this post office?
No.

While we are on that question, I would direct the minister's attention to the fact that special men are employed to look after these clocks where they have been put in. For example, at Ingersoll we paid for the care of the clock for one year $25. In London, we pay $50. And it appears that we paid for the same gentleman who takes care of the clock, for cleaning and repairing, $100, besides the year's salary. In Hamilton, Thomas Lee is paid $65 per annum for the care of clock. Each of these buildings has a caretaker at a reasonable salary. As these are eight-day clocks, could not the caretaker wind them up without employing a special man at $50 or $60 a year?

I think the hon. gentleman is misinformed as to the salaries of the caretakers. The salaries paid those who take care of these small buildings amount to $300 or $400, and nobody would say that was a large salary. We have found it necessary to make payments to persons to look after the clocks in these buildings, and the salaries range from $25 to $50, as a rule. The clocks require careful looking after.
Would it not be better to increase the salary of the caretaker and have him spend ten minutes every week in winding the clock?
In some cases we do allow the caretaker an extra amount for his services. I have in mind now such a case. No doubt, it is desirable, where the caretaker is able to do it.
Where a public building has been erected, I do not think it is asking too much of the municipality to bear the expense of taking care of it.

The minister is right. The earetaker, as a rule, is not competent to wind the clock. The clock has to be wound and cared for by a practical clockmaker. In London, since the man who had it in charge refused to wind it, the clock has been allowed to stop. There is no use in the government putting in good clocks and not looking after them, and to pay a man $50 is not too much for that service. I have listened to a good deal of talk on this Mr. WALLACE.
side of the House this evening. Part of it was with regard to Glencoe. Glencoe is in Middlesex county, which is one of the very best counties in this country, and it is the one I have the honour to live in. One hon. member said that Glencoe had only one railway. I did not want to contradict him, but, as a matter of fact, they have the Grand Trunk, the Wabash and also the Canadian Pacific Railway. Glencoe is a smart little town in one of the best districts in Ontario. Glencoe is deserving of a post office. And I understand it is to have the military building also in connection?
Yes.

The hon. member who made reference to Glencoe is not in his seat. But the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie) must not forget that the minister has already stated that the policy of the government is, in many towns, to employ the caretaker and increase his salary by a few dollars.
I said that was done in a few cases ^rhere the caretaker was competent.
The hon. gentleman said it required a competent clockmaker.
That is the kind of man we do employ.

As to the salaries of caretakers, I do not wish to say they are excessive, but, in the average town of 3,000 or
4,000	population, the caretaker of the public building is paid $500 a year. In my own town, for instance, the salary is $500, with free house, free heating, free lighting and some other things I could mention. And the caretaker took an active part in the ejections.
How large a town is it?
About 4,000 people.
In the smaller towns, the salary is from $300 to $400.

I have a list before me, and if the hon. gentleman will look at it, he will see that the figures are correct. I am directing attention to this one case. The caretaker of this place is an active politician, so active that he drove around and collected the ballot-boxes in my county after the election was over.
Did not they store the boxes in. the post office?

They occupied a room in the post office-that is correct. But that has nothing to do with the caretaker. I did not assume that his duties were to drive to every polling subdivision in the county to gather up the ballot-boxes. If it is so, we would all like to know it. The policy of the government has been stated to be, in accordance with the resolution of this

House, that these employees may vote, but are not to take an active part in the elections. May I ask the minister, on the clock question, whether it is the policy of the government to engage competent watchmakers to wind up these clocks?

Yes, that is the policy.
I had in my mind the case of Moncton, where the caretaker has been engaged to do that work. I think there are other places where the same thing is done. But the general rule is to employ practical jewellers.
Ottawa-Building for testing of fuel by Department of Mines, $15,000.

This building is for the purpose of testing the commercial value of peat for producing gas. The machinery is being brought from the old country, and is being installed under the direction of Dr. Haanel. A requisition has been made upon my department by the Minister of Mines for the erection of this building. We have purchased a site, and we now ask for $15,000 for the purpose of completing the building. Of this $15,000, $8,000 is a revote.
Where is the building to be put?
We have bought a lot of land, about half an acre, on Concession street, in the southwestern part of the city.
I suppose that when a demand is made on the Department of Public Works by another department the minister has nothing to say, but he must grant the request.

I could refuse, as Minister of Public Works, but the hon. gentleman will see that it is my duty to pay the greatest respect to a requisition from another department. I wish to reply to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) with regard to these caretakers. In Amherst we pay $400, in Antigonish $400, in Annapolis 400, in Arichat $150, in Baddeck $250, in Canso, $350, in Dartmouth, $250. Another is $400, another $50.
Are there any higher than $400?
Some are as high as $500, in two or three instances they run up to $700.
Where a salary of $400 is paid, does that include a house, heating and lighting?
Yes.
How much does the minister expect this new building for testing peat will cost, including everything?
We expect $15,000 will cover the entire expense, not including machinery.

I was going to suggest to the minister to let this item stand.
I would like to discuss it at some length, but the hour is getting late, and I have to leave at 11 o'clock. I wanted to enter my protest against this expenditure being made at all, because it is a well known fact that in Europe people have been using peat successfully as fuel, and to produce gas, for the last twenty years. There is nothing new at all in this suggestion of the director of the Bureau of Mines. There is no need for this government to be paying out good money to repeat experiments that have been going on in Europe for years.
I would like to have information as to what the government wishes to do in this matter, how they are going to expend the money; I would like full details.
This question could more properly be discussed when we come to the estimates of the Minister of Mines The hon. gentleman will then be afforded full opportunity.

There are 500 gas producing plants now at work in Canada.
I do not wish to let the item go through without full discussion. I think the government should strike that item out.
We are committed to this.' We have bought the property, and we must ask the item to pass.

It seems to me my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has a perfect right to ask that this item be allowed to stand if he objects to it, and wishes to discuss it later. Surely that is what this committee is for.
The hon. gentleman can go right on and discuss it now if he wishes.
I am asking for some information.
If the hon. gentleman requires information about this matter, surely he is entitled to it.

Parliament has already expressed its approval of this enterprise last session, without a dissenting voice. The land has actually been purchased, the machinery has actually been purchased, and I presume it is now in Ottawa ready to be placed in the building. Therefore my hon. friend must see that no matter what might be his persuasive powers, I would have to ask this committee to pass the vote because we are already committed to it. I would again suggest to my hon. friend that he can discuss this question when the estimates of the Minister of Mines are taken up, or he can discuss it this evening.
My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) asks for some information that the minister has not in his possession at the moment. I would like to know who is responsible for that.
I do not want to he unreasonable about it. How long would my hon. friend like the item to stand?
Until Monday.
I am willing.
I intended asking many questions about gas producer tanks and other things that the minister might not understand and it would be an advantage if he had all the information.

This $15,000 is for use in the testing of a system of gas peat production. The question of obtaining a cheap fuel has been a live issue in this country, especially in Ontario, for many years. Many attempts have been made to manufacture peat into fuel, and it was discovered that a German inventor has the best producer gas plant for using peat known. This government, I am glad to say, has already purchased one of these producers and this $15,000 is to erect a building for it._ The machinery is all ready, and I think this will be one of the best investments that Canada has made in many years. I feel that in a year or two through these experiments we will find the means of obtaining cheap power and fuel in this northern country where we have no coal.

This is for fittings for the departmental oflices. It is about the same as for other years. Latterly we are endeavouring to put in steel fittings which are fire proof and very much safer. This appropriation is likely to be continued until the last trumpet shall sound.
The fittings appear to be nearly all supplied by one or two companies. Are tenders called?

Only two firms in Canada manufacture these goods. The chief architect made inquiry at Washington, where they have adopted these very generally, and acquainted himself with the price there, and from time to time tenders have been invited from these two companies for the different fittings. Prices have been got from them and they have been accepted where the chief architect from his experience thought they were fair and reasonable.
-Ottawa-Lepartmental Buildings-Improvements in lavatories, plumbing, &c., $10,000.
Why is not. this in item 138?

This is rather special work.
Simcoe-Public Buildings, $20,000.
The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. A. McCall )has asked me to inquire as to the cost of the site and building here.
The site cost $2,050. The whole lot is 80.3 feet by 102. It seems very moderate. The estimated total cost is about $38,000.
Is it intended to erect a tower and put a clock in it?
I think not; it is not intended to do so.
Why is it that the people in Nova Scotia in these little places, Amherst, Bridgewater, Guysborough and New Glasgow, all require towers and clocks, and in Ontario they do not seem to require any?

In some towns they want one class of buildings, in others a different class. The people of Simcoe desired a-building of a classic design; it is one story building with cut stone trimmings, and they did not ask for a tower.
Is it the policy of the minister to erect these buildings in whatever style some people in a town suggest.

As a rule we confer with the member representing the constituency and with the leading men who take sufficient interest to come to Ottawa to make representations. We are glad to receive suggestions from any respectable citizen. Of course where we have a large lot and the building can be set back from the street it may be desirable to adopt a different design from that which would be adopted if the building were built close up to the sidewalk. All these things must be taken into consideration.
I dont see why you require a clock and a tower in one place and why you do not in another
Do you ask for a clock on this building ?
Can you tell me what person in Simcoe suggested there should not be a tower and clock on this building?
Do you complain there is no clock ?
I am asking you the question.

I don't know.
Whitby-Public Buildings, $28,000.
How much did the site cost ?
Is not that a high price for a lot in a small town like Whitby ?

The lot is exceedingly well situated with a frontage on one street of sixty-five feet and on another of 150 feet. The inspector made a very careful inquiry and interviewed citizens on both sides of politics and his information was that $5,000 was a fair and reasonable price.
What will be the total cost of the Whitby building?
$33,000 estimated.
Will the minister bring down a list of the newspapers in which an advertisement was inserted for the buildings in the towns of Welland, Whitby, and Simcoe, with the amount paid to each paper ?
I shall.
Would he also state what are the politics of each paper.

I will leave that for you to judge.
